evidence: Statement a is about how widely the methodology applies: one agent, a system of agents, a company, or a group of companies. Statement b is about its internal structure: intent at the top, communication at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality between them. Neither limits the other. Example: one methodology has exactly those five layers in that order. A single agent uses it to turn an intent into tasks, check its capability, assess quality and report results. The same five layers are used to coordinate a multi-agent system, a whole company and a group of companies. That example meets every clause of both statements.

Both can hold in one scenario. Statement a says the methodology resolves tasks at every listed scale: a single agent, a system of agents, a company and a group of companies. Statement b sets the framing: tasks are the problem, capability is the means of resolving them, and quality is the standard the work is judged against. Example: a methodology treats each task as a problem, applies the available capability to resolve it, and judges the result against quality criteria. It does this both for one agent fixing a bug and for a group of companies delivering a joint project. Nothing in b restricts scale, and nothing in a conflicts with b's framing, so every clause of both is satisfied.

Statement a is about the scope of the methodology: it applies at every scale, from one agent to a group of companies. Statement b is about where tasks come from: a request, a need, or maintenance, because the environment changes. Neither limits the other. Example: the methodology handles a user's request for one agent, a need-driven task for a multi-agent system, maintenance of a company's ordering process as conditions shift, and a cross-company request in a holding group. Every task arises in one of b's three ways, the environment is alive, and the methodology resolves tasks at each scale named in a.

Both can hold at once. Example: a methodology applied to one agent, a multi-agent system, a single company and a group of companies. At every one of these scales, its task-organising step breaks tasks into subtasks (decomposition), maps which tasks depend on others (dependencies), ranks them (prioritisation) and sorts them into categories (classification). Statement a only claims the methodology works at every scale. Statement b only lists what organising tasks covers. Neither restricts the other, so nothing conflicts.

The statements address different things and do not conflict. (a) says the methodology works at every scale; (b) says what task management includes. Example satisfying both: a methodology is applied to one agent, a multi-agent system, a single company and a group of companies, and resolves tasks at each level. At every level, managing a task means executing it, verifying the result and measuring outcomes. Both hold together.

Both statements can hold for the same methodology. Example: a methodology built on decomposition is applied to a group of companies' goal. That goal is split into company-level tasks, then team or agent-system tasks, then single-agent tasks. Each task at each level has its own intent, capability and quality, which satisfies b's recursive decomposition. The same procedure works whether the starting task belongs to a single agent, a system of agents, a company or a group of companies, which satisfies a's claim that it resolves tasks at any scale. Recursion actually supports scale-independence, so nothing conflicts.

The two statements fit together. A says the methodology works at every scale. B describes what happens when work is split and handed down between those scales. Concrete example: a group of companies uses the methodology for a project. It delegates a subtask to one company, which becomes a new working group. That company inherits the shared language and channels and renegotiates its own meeting moments, commitments and exceptions. The company then delegates part of the work to a multi-agent system, and that system hands a piece to a single agent. Each handoff again inherits the base and adjusts the local parts. Here the methodology resolves tasks at every scale named in A, and every delegation follows B's rule. Nothing in either statement rules this out.

Statement a says the methodology resolves tasks at any scale (single agent, agent system, company, group of companies). Statement b says that in each task, autonomy is a goal rather than a standard or a whole, and its boundary is set by the agreement's exceptions. Concrete example: the methodology is applied to one agent's task and to a company-wide task. In each, autonomy is pursued as a goal, not imposed as a fixed standard. Its limits are whatever exceptions the governing agreement lists, for example 'no autonomous spending above $X'. The methodology still resolves both tasks. Neither statement restricts the other's scope, so every clause of both holds.

A claims the methodology handles tasks at any scale, from one agent to a group of companies. B is a table that pairs quality figures (form, fit, economy, completeness, order, sharpness, truthfulness) with an image and a kind of slop in the work, such as a term used before its definition. B says nothing about scale, so it neither limits nor denies A. Concrete example: one methodology document states it applies equally to a single agent, an agent system, a company and a group of companies, and it contains this table as its checklist for spotting slop. Both statements hold in full.

The two statements address different things and fit together. Example: a methodology is applied to tasks run by a single agent, by multi-agent systems, by a company and by a group of companies, so it resolves tasks at any scale. Within that methodology, the comparison loop is handed off as a delegated task under its own agreement. It runs autonomously internally, and the user validates its output at the end. Statement b describing one delegated sub-task with end-of-task user validation does not limit the scales at which the methodology works, so every clause of both holds.

Statement b is a question. It asserts nothing, except perhaps the presupposition that quality belongs either to the result or to the task-result relation. Nothing in a conflicts with either answer. Concrete example: a methodology M resolves tasks for a single agent, a multi-agent system, a company and a group of companies, which satisfies every scale listed in a. Separately, quality is defined as the relation between a task and its result, which answers b's question and satisfies its presupposition. Choosing 'quality is a property of the result' instead works equally well. Both statements hold together.

Example: a team's working methodology rests on a communication agreement, and every other practice is defined on top of it (b). The methodology's review-and-revision rules also apply to that agreement and to the review rules themselves, so nothing is exempt (a). A foundation can still be subject to the method built on it. Being foundational does not mean being exempt, so every clause of both statements holds.

The two statements cover different matters: (a) says what the methodology applies to, and (b) says when a group settles its agreement. Example: a working group forms and, as its first act, settles its agreement. The methodology governs that agreement just as it governs every other part of itself, including its own rules, so nothing is exempt. Settling the agreement first does not exempt it from the methodology, and applying the methodology to the agreement does not stop it from being settled first. Every clause of both statements holds.

Example: a team's agreement has six sections. Language: shared terms. Channels: chat and email. Format: a written template. Moments: a weekly sync. Commitments: response within 24h. Exceptions: in emergencies, a phone call replaces chat. The methodology is applied to itself and to this agreement, and every section, including the Exceptions section, is reviewed and governed by it. No part is exempt. Having an 'exceptions' component means handling exceptional situations inside the agreement. It does not exempt any part from the methodology, so every clause of both statements holds.

Example: a methodology requires every artefact to be monitored and verified. It applies that rule to its own text and to its agreements, with nothing exempt. Its agreement is monitored and verified like any other artefact, and it has no expiry date or usage limit, so it stays in force indefinitely. This satisfies a: the methodology applies to itself and its agreements, and no part is exempt. It satisfies b: the agreement is treated like other artefacts and does not expire. Neither statement says the methodology requires artefacts to expire, so non-expiry is not an exemption from any stated rule.

Both can hold at once. Example: a methodology governs all of its parts and its own agreements, with none exempt. One of its own agreements fails a verification. Under the methodology's rules, that agreement is reviewed. The review finds a defect, so the agreement is updated. Statement a is met because the methodology's own agreement gets no exemption from the process. Statement b is met because the failed verification leads to a review, and the defect found leads to an update. Nothing in either statement forbids this.

Example: a team's methodology contains the delegation rule from b. When the team splits off a subtask, the new subgroup keeps the same language and channels and adjusts its own meeting moments, commitments and exceptions. When the methodology itself is revised, for instance by delegating the drafting of a new version, that work also forms a subgroup under the same rule: it inherits the base and adjusts its local parts. The methodology's own agreements are reviewed by the methodology. So the methodology applies to itself and its agreements with no part exempt, as a requires, and each delegated level inherits or renegotiates its agreement, as b requires. Inheriting the base does not exempt it: inheritance is how the methodology is applied at that level, and a does not require every part to be renegotiated at every level.

Example: methodology M applies to its own rules and to every agreement made under it, with no part exempt. One such agreement says that in each task the goal is to act autonomously. Autonomy is not treated as a general standard or as the whole of the work. The agreement lists exceptions, such as 'spending over $500 needs approval', and these mark where autonomy stops. The exceptions are themselves clauses of an agreement governed by M, so they are reviewed under M like everything else. They limit autonomy; they do not exempt any part from M. Both statements hold.

The two statements address different things and fit together. Example: a methodology M includes a rule that the possible responses to any diagnosis are accept, accept with reservations, correct, escalate, or review the agreement or the intent. M is applied to everything, including M itself and its own agreements, with no part exempt. When a diagnosis targets one of M's own agreements, the party responds with one of the five listed options, for instance 'review the agreement'. This satisfies a, because M's agreements are subject to M. It also satisfies b, because the response comes from the fixed list. Neither statement limits the other's scope or count.

Example: a team methodology contains an agreement on code-review timing. A minor timing deviation is judged tolerable, so the team resolves it locally, at the agreement's own level. A deviation that breaks a release commitment is judged intolerable and goes to the steering group. The same escalation rule is applied to the methodology's own meta-agreements: a small wording dispute about the rule is settled within that meta-agreement, while a dispute that would undermine it is escalated. This satisfies (a), because the methodology and its own agreements, including the escalation rule, are all subject to the methodology with no part exempt. It satisfies (b), because tolerable matters stay at their own level, intolerable ones escalate, and tolerability sets the limit of local autonomy. Local resolution is itself an application of the methodology, not an exemption from it, so the two statements do not conflict.

Example: the methodology lets a delegated task run autonomously and requires user validation at the end. The comparison loop is such a task. Its agreement is written and governed under the methodology's own rules, like every other part, so nothing is exempt (a). The loop then runs without user intervention and the user validates the result at the end (b). 'Autonomous inside' means no mid-task user involvement, not freedom from the methodology. So both statements hold.

Example: a methodology with five layers. Intent is at the top, communication is at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality sit between them. Communication is the foundational layer, the agreement between parties, and the other four parts (intent included) are built on it. This satisfies a's five parts and their order. It also satisfies b, because communication 'beneath' everything is the substrate, and 'built on the agreement' fits the colon's reading of the agreement as what communication establishes. Being 'above' does not stop intent from resting on that base.

Example: a methodology with five layers. Intent sits at the top, communication at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality in between. Intent is the purpose that gives meaning to the other four parts. Statement a's placement of intent 'above' fits b's 'above everything'. B's claim that intent gives meaning to everything else is additional detail, not a conflict with a's structure.

Both can hold in one methodology. Statement a sets out five parts: intent at the top, communication at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality in the middle. Statement b only says what the three middle parts do: tasks are the problem, capability is the means to resolve it, and quality is what the work is judged against. Nothing in b changes the count or the layering in a. A methodology built with that layered structure and those three meanings for the middle parts satisfies every clause of both statements.

Example: a methodology with exactly five parts. Intent is the top layer, communication is the bottom layer, and tasks, capability and quality sit between them. That satisfies a. Because communication is the base layer, it is foundational. Every relation between parts, such as intent to tasks or capability to quality, is carried through communication, so it is cross-cutting and the medium of every relation rather than merely a channel. That satisfies b. Being 'beneath' fits 'foundational', and a base layer can still pervade all relations. Neither statement requires communication to be confined to one position or excluded from the others.

The statements describe different things. Statement a counts the methodology's parts: intent on top, communication at the base, and tasks, capability and quality between them. Statement b classifies the relations within the methodology, saying every one is a form of communication. Both can hold at once. Example: a methodology has exactly those five layers, with communication as the base layer that carries every interaction. Distilling intent into tasks is downward communication. Verifying or reporting a result is upward. Consulting a peer is lateral. Written know-how is communication deferred in time. Regulation is a judgement already made and passed on. Communication being one named part does not stop every relation from being communication. Statement b's list of relations does not add parts or change a's count of five.

The two statements cover different things. Statement a lists the methodology's five parts: intent, tasks, capability, quality and communication at the base. Statement b lists properties of a single communication. Both hold in this example: a methodology has exactly those five parts in that order, and every communication within it has a fidelity, a shared language, a direction, a timing (immediate or deferred) and a recipient (person, agent or environment). Describing a communication's properties neither changes the number of parts nor adds a part.

Example: an organisation with team, department and company levels uses a five-part methodology. Intent sits above, communication sits beneath, and tasks, capability and quality sit between them. At each organisational level (team, department, company), that level sets its own intent within the intent part. This satisfies every clause of a (five parts in the stated arrangement) and of b (intent is set at each level). Statement b does not say the 'levels' are the five parts. It also does not say intent stops being the top part, so the two statements do not conflict.

Statement b does not say what its 'levels' are, so they need not be the five parts of statement a. Example: a methodology has five parts. Intent is at the top, communication at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality sit between them. Within it, intent is set at nested levels: organisation, then team, then individual. Each level's intent adds to the intent of the level above in order to fulfil it, rather than copying it exactly. This satisfies every clause of both statements, and neither rules the other out.

Example: a methodology has five layers. Intent is at the top, communication at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality sit between them. The top-level intent is refined at each layer as it passes down: tasks, capability, quality and communication each carry a more condensed form of it. That satisfies a's five-part structure and ordering, and b's distillation of intent from level to level. Intent being one named part does not stop it from being carried and distilled across the levels.

Both can hold at once. Example: a methodology has exactly five parts, stacked as intent, then tasks, capability and quality, then communication. Within the quality part there is a verification activity. It checks that a team-level result meets the team's intent, and that the team's intent still serves the organisation-level intent above it. Statement b does not say verification is a sixth part, and its 'levels' can be levels of work rather than the five parts. So neither statement's requirements are violated.

The statements cover different things and can both hold. A describes a five-part methodology: intent at the top, communication at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality between them. B says drift can empty the original intent of meaning. Example: a project uses exactly those five layers. Over months the tasks shift away from what was first meant, so the stated intent at the top still exists but no longer means anything. Both statements are satisfied; A's structure does not rule out drift, and B only asserts a possibility.

Example: a methodology has exactly five parts. Intent sits at the top, communication at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality lie between them. Within it, a task such as 'update a dependency' arises for maintenance, another arises because a user requested it, and a third arises from an identified need. All of this happens because the environment keeps changing ('alive'). Statement a fixes the methodology's structure; statement b describes how tasks originate and why. Neither restricts the other, so both hold.

Both can hold in one example. Take a methodology with exactly five parts. Intent sits at the top and communication at the bottom. Between them are tasks, capability and quality. Within the tasks part, organising tasks is defined as decomposition, dependencies, prioritisation and classification. This meets every clause of a: five parts in the stated arrangement. It also meets b. Statement b only says what organising tasks covers; it adds no part or count that conflicts with a. Even if 'organising tasks' is not the same as a's 'tasks' part, b sets no limit that clashes with a's structure.

Example: a methodology has five parts, with intent at the top, communication at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality in between. The tasks part covers execution, verification and measurement. The quality part covers something else, such as standards and review criteria. Statement a only lists the parts and their order. It never assigns verification or measurement to quality or forbids tasks from covering them. Statement b only describes what managing tasks covers. Both statements hold together.

Example: a problem-solving way of thinking called decomposition is the methodology. It has five parts: intent at the top, communication at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality between them. Any task can split into subtasks, and each subtask again has its own intent, capability and quality, so the methodology is recursive. This satisfies a's five-part structure and b's claims that decomposition is the methodology and that it recurses. b not mentioning communication for subtasks does not deny it, and calling the methodology 'decomposition' does not conflict with it having five parts.

The two statements describe different things, so they can hold together. Statement a lists the five parts of the methodology: intent on top, communication at the base, and tasks, capability and quality in between. Statement b describes the working agreement and what happens to it when a task is delegated: the base (language, channels) is inherited and the local parts (moments, commitments, exceptions) are adjusted. Those are parts of an agreement, not extra parts of the methodology, so the count of five is unaffected. Example: a team uses the five-part methodology. One task is split and handed to a sub-team, which forms a new working group. That group keeps the same language and channels but sets its own meeting moments, commitments and exception rules. Every clause of both statements is satisfied.

Example: a methodology has exactly five parts arranged as described: intent at the top, communication at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality in between. Within the tasks part, every task names autonomy as one of its goals. Autonomy is not treated as a standard, so it is not part of quality, and it is not a whole, so it is not a sixth part. The agreement lists exceptions, and those exceptions mark where each task's autonomy ends. Statement b places autonomy inside the tasks part, so the five-part count and order in a stay unchanged. Every clause of both statements holds.

Statement a sets out a five-part methodology. Intent is on top, communication is at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality sit in between. Statement b only says that capability is either intrinsic or extrinsic to the executor. Nothing in a rules out either option. Concrete example: a methodology layered intent / tasks / capability / quality / communication, where the capability layer covers the executor's own skills and knowledge. That makes capability intrinsic, which satisfies b's disjunction while all of a's structure holds.

Example: a methodology has exactly five parts. Intent is at the top and communication at the bottom. Tasks, capability and quality sit between them. Within the capability part, 'intrinsic capability' is defined as power, speed and context management. Statement b only breaks down one concept into components. It does not add or remove top-level parts, so a's count of five and its ordering are untouched.

Example: a methodology has exactly five parts. Intent sits at the top, communication at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality lie between them. Within the capability part, extrinsic capability is defined as know-how. The analogy is that a person corresponds to the model, while documents, courses and regulations are the know-how and belong to the organisation. Statement a fixes the count and order of the parts. Statement b only defines one kind of capability and gives an analogy, and nothing in it changes the number or placement of the parts. Both hold.

Statement a lists the methodology's five parts: intent on top, communication at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality between them. Statement b never claims normative know-how is a sixth part. It only says normative know-how limits capability rather than extending it, and connects directly with quality. Concrete example: a methodology with exactly those five parts, plus a body of normative know-how (such as standards and rules) that sits outside it or within one of its parts. That know-how restricts what capability may do and links straight to quality. Every clause of both statements holds.

Both can hold at once. Example: a methodology with exactly five parts, ordered intent (top), then tasks, capability and quality in the middle, then communication (bottom). Inside the quality part, constraints, verification and monitoring are produced as derived elements. None of them is an independent starting point or a sixth part. Statement a fixes the five parts and their layout. Statement b only says those three items come from quality and are not origins, which fits with quality being one of the five parts. Nothing in a requires constraints, verification or monitoring to be separate parts or starting points.

Statement a counts the methodology's parts, and quality is one of the five. Statement b lists six attributes of quality, so it describes the inside of that one part. These counts are at different levels and do not clash. Concrete example: a methodology ordered intent, tasks, capability, quality, communication (five parts, with intent on top, communication at the bottom and the other three between them), where the quality part is defined by fitness for purpose, verifiability, performance, security, resilience and maintainability. This satisfies every clause of both statements.

The statements are about different things: a lists the five parts of the methodology, and b lists the possible responses to a diagnosis. Neither limits the other. Example: a framework whose methodology has intent at the top, communication at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality between them. In that framework, a diagnosis can be met by accepting, accepting with reservations, correcting, escalating, or reviewing the agreement or the intent. Every clause of both statements holds in this example.

Statement a says the methodology has five parts: intent, tasks, capability, quality and communication. Statement b is a table of seven 'figures' (form, fit, economy, completeness, order, sharpness, truthfulness), each paired with an image and the kinds of slop it catches in the work. Statement b never says these seven figures are the methodology's parts, so the counts do not clash. Example satisfying both: a methodology with exactly the five parts in a's order (intent above, communication beneath, and tasks, capability and quality between them). Its quality part uses the seven figures in b's table to judge the work. Under that part, an element 'not traceable to the intent' counts as a misfit, and 'a task without verification' counts as incomplete. b's references to intent and tasks fit a's structure, and nothing in a rules out b's table.

The two statements describe different things and do not conflict. Statement a fixes the methodology's structure: five parts, with intent on top, communication at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality between them. Statement b describes one task, the comparison loop. Concrete example: a methodology has exactly those five parts in that arrangement. Within its tasks part, the comparison loop is delegated under its own agreement, runs autonomously, and is validated by the user at the end. Every clause of both statements holds, and neither statement prohibits what the other asserts.

b is a question, so it asserts nothing that could conflict with a. Its only presupposition is that something called quality exists and can be discussed. a supports that by listing quality among the five parts. Example: a methodology document puts intent at the top and communication at the bottom, with tasks, capability and quality between them. A reader of that document then asks whether its 'quality' part describes the result itself or the fit between task and result. Every clause of a holds, and b is a coherent question about it. The question stays open, because a does not settle which answer is right.

Statement b is a question, so it asserts nothing that could conflict with a. Its presuppositions can still hold alongside a. Concrete example: a methodology has five parts, with intent at the top, communication at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality in between. Its quality part separates product quality (judged on the outputs) from process quality (judged on how tasks are carried out). Both are measured along dimensions such as accuracy and timeliness. Someone then asks b about this methodology. Every clause of a holds, and b's question and its assumptions fit this setup.

Example: in a distributed system, the message protocol is the base layer, and every component is built on the agreed protocol. That satisfies a: communication is the substrate and everything rests on the agreement. Every interaction between components happens through messages, not just one designated data link. That satisfies b: communication is foundational, cross-cutting, the medium of every relation and more than a channel. 'Substrate' (base layer) and 'cross-cutting' (spanning everything) do not conflict, because a foundation can also run through every relation. b explicitly calls communication foundational too. 'The agreement' in a is unspecified, but reading it as the agreement reached through communication fits b.

Both can hold in the same scenario. Example: a new working group forms. Its first act is to settle its agreement, a shared communication protocol covering channels, vocabulary and how decisions are recorded. That satisfies b. All later work, including task assignments, designs and deliverables, is built on that agreement, and communication serves as the substrate. That satisfies a. Settling the agreement first fits with everything else resting on it, so no requirement conflicts.

The two statements do not conflict. Example: a team's communication agreement has exactly six components: language (English), channels (Slack and email), format (written summaries), moments (daily standup), commitments (reply within 24h) and exceptions (urgent issues by phone). All of the team's other processes are built on that agreement, so communication is their substrate. Statement a says what rests on the agreement, and statement b says what the agreement contains. Both hold at once.

Example: a methodology rests on communication, and the agreements reached through it underpin everything else, as a requires. Its relations are all forms of communication, as b requires: distilling intent goes downward, verifying or reporting a result goes upward, consulting another is lateral, written know-how is communication deferred in time, and regulation is a judgement already made. Saying communication is the substrate (a) fits with classifying every relation as communication (b). Those relations can be communication while other things, such as artifacts or results, are built on the agreement. Nothing in either statement excludes the other.

Example: a team's communication protocol agreement is the foundation on which every other artefact (code, tests, docs) is built. The agreement is kept under version control and checked by the same monitoring and verification pipeline as those other artefacts. It has no expiry date or usage limit. Statement a needs only that the agreement is foundational; b needs only that it is monitored and verified like other artefacts and never expires. Being foundational does not exempt something from verification, and the verification tooling can itself be built on the agreement it checks. Every clause of both statements holds.

Example: a team treats communication as its foundation, and every plan and process rests on a shared working agreement. One week the agreement fails a verification check, so the team reviews it. The review finds a defect, and the team updates the agreement. Statement a says what everything is built on. Statement b sets two conditional steps for handling failures and defects. Building on the agreement does not stop it from being reviewed or updated, so every clause of both statements holds.

Statement a says communication is the foundation and everything else rests on the agreement. Statement b lists attributes a communication has. Neither excludes the other. Example: a team builds its whole workflow on one agreed message. That message has high fidelity, uses shared English, flows one way from lead to agent, is delivered immediately and goes to an agent. That communication is the substrate, satisfying a, and it has every property b lists, satisfying b. The unclear referent of 'the agreement' in a does not affect this, since b places no constraint on what is built on it.

Example: a team's agreement fixes a shared language and channels, plus meeting times, commitments and exception handling. All work is coordinated through that agreement, which satisfies a: communication is the substrate and everything else is built on the agreement. The lead splits a project and delegates a subtask, forming a new subgroup. That subgroup keeps the same language and channels (inherited) and sets its own check-in times, commitments and exceptions (adjusted). This satisfies b at each level. The subgroup's work still rests on an agreement, partly inherited and partly renegotiated, so a still holds. b only says how the agreement propagates through delegation, which adds detail without denying a.

Example: a team's working agreement is the foundation that communication rests on, and every process, role and practice is built on it. Each task aims at autonomy. Autonomy is not a team-wide standard or a single whole, and its limits are the exceptions listed in the agreement (for example, 'escalate if budget exceeds X'). This satisfies (a), because everything, autonomy included, is built on the agreement. It satisfies (b), because autonomy is a per-task goal, not a standard or a whole, bounded by the agreement's exceptions. Nothing in (b) requires autonomy to stand outside the agreement, so the two fit together.

Example: a team's process rests on communication and a shared agreement from which all its practices derive. When a diagnosis is issued, the only allowed responses are accept, accept with reservations, correct, escalate, or review the agreement or the intent. Statement a says what the process is founded on. Statement b fixes the set of responses to a diagnosis. Neither restricts the other, and 'review the agreement' fits a process built on that agreement.

Example: a team sets up a working agreement through communication. Every process, including its escalation rules, is defined by that agreement, so communication is the substrate and everything else rests on the agreement. Under it, a minor schedule slip is judged tolerable and the team resolves it itself. A serious breach is judged intolerable and is escalated to management. The team's autonomy extends exactly as far as what is tolerable. Statement a describes the foundation, and statement b describes how issues are handled within it, so every clause of both holds.

Example: the user and the agent communicate and settle an overall agreement, and all later work rests on it. Within that agreement they agree to delegate a comparison loop with its own sub-agreement covering scope and success criteria. The loop runs autonomously, and the user validates the result at the end. The loop's own agreement is built on the main agreement, so 'everything else is built on the agreement' still holds. Internal autonomy does not remove communication as the substrate, because the delegation was agreed through communication and the final validation is also communication.

Example: a methodology in which intent sits at the top and gives every activity its purpose. Distilling that intent is communication flowing downward, verifying or reporting results flows upward toward it, consulting peers is lateral, written know-how is communication deferred in time, and regulation is a judgement already made. Every relation is communication, satisfying b, while intent stays above everything and gives meaning to the rest, satisfying a. Classifying relations as communication does not rank anything above intent, and the 'downward' direction of distilling intent fits intent being at the top.

Read 'above everything' as 'takes priority over everything.' Example: in a military command structure, intent is the overriding guide that gives meaning to every order and action. Each echelon (army, brigade, company) also states its own intent. Intent is then paramount and gives meaning to everything else (a), and it is set at each level (b). 'Above everything' describes importance, not a single place in a hierarchy, so intent being present at every level does not lower its priority.

Example: in a military organisation, intent is the top priority and gives meaning to every plan, order and action. The commander's intent sits at the top. Each subordinate level forms its own intent, which is not a strict copy but adds to the level above in order to fulfil it. This satisfies a, since intent outranks and gives meaning to everything else. It satisfies b, since intent is passed down non-strictly, with each level complementing and fulfilling the one above. Statement a ranks intent above everything that is not intent. Statement b describes how intents relate to each other across levels, so the two do not conflict.

Example: in a military command structure, the commander's intent ranks above every plan and order and gives each of them its meaning. That satisfies a. As it passes down each echelon, the intent is distilled, condensed and refined for the next level. That satisfies b. Being supreme and meaning-giving does not stop intent from being refined across levels, so both statements hold in one scenario.

Example: a product team sets an overarching intent (e.g. 'help users file taxes easily'). It sits above everything and gives every plan, task and check its meaning. Below it are nested level intents: a feature intent ('guided form entry') and a component intent ('validate each field'). Verification takes a field-validator result and confirms it fulfils the component intent. It then confirms that this component intent still serves the feature intent above it. Statement b's ranking of intents among themselves does not put intent below anything non-intent. Intent as such remains above everything and supplies meaning, verification included, so both statements hold.

Example: a team treats intent as its top priority, and intent is what gives purpose to all its other activities. Over the years its original intent ('serve rural patients') drifts into a slogan that no longer means anything. The team then adopts a new intent, which again ranks above everything and gives meaning to its work. Statement a holds: intent is supreme and confers meaning on everything else. Statement b holds: drift emptied the original intent of meaning. The two do not clash. Statement a ranks intent's importance and names it as the source of meaning for 'everything else', a phrase that excludes intent itself. It never says intent's own meaning is immune to erosion. Statement b only says such erosion is possible, and only for the 'original' intent.

Example: a framework ranks intent above everything and has it give meaning to all other elements. Its working methodology is decomposition, a problem-solving way of thinking that is subordinate to intent. Decomposition makes the method recursive: a task splits into subtasks, and each subtask has its own intent, capability and quality. Within each subtask, that subtask's intent gives meaning to its capability and quality, and it in turn serves the parent intent. Calling decomposition 'the methodology' does not rank it above intent, and every task having its own intent reinforces intent's primacy. Every clause of both statements holds.

Both can hold in one framework. Example: in a governance model, intent is the supreme reference that gives meaning to every other element. When a diagnosis is produced, the possible responses are accept, accept with reservations, correct, escalate, or review the agreement or the intent. Being 'above everything' gives intent priority and makes it the source of meaning. It does not say intent can never be re-examined, and treating it as unrevisable would add a prohibition that statement a does not state. Reviewing the intent does not stop intent from being above everything else or from giving meaning to it.

Both can hold in one work. Example: a specification states its intent first and judges every other element by it. It uses b's table as its quality checklist: forms, fit, economy, completeness, order, sharpness and truthfulness, each with the listed image and slop examples. Nothing in b ranks anything above intent or denies that intent gives meaning to other elements. b's 'fit' row even treats 'an element not traceable to the intent' as slop, which fits a's claim that intent is primary.

Both statements can hold in one concrete case. A user requests a broken report export be fixed (a task arising on request). The broken export is the problem. A developer's debugging skill is the means used to resolve it. The fix is judged against quality criteria such as correct output and no regressions. The environment is alive: users keep making requests, and dependencies drift and need maintenance, which is why such tasks keep arising. Statement a defines the roles of task, capability and quality. Statement b explains where tasks come from. Neither restricts the other, so every clause of both is satisfied.

Example: a project framework treats each task as the problem to solve, uses team capability (skills, tools) as the means to resolve it, and judges finished work against quality standards. Separately, organising those tasks means breaking them into subtasks, mapping dependencies, ranking priority and classifying them by type. Statement a defines the roles of tasks, capability and quality. Statement b describes what organising tasks involves. Neither restricts the other, so this example satisfies both.

The two statements fit together. Example: a team's task is fixing a login bug, which is the problem. The engineers' skills are the capability used to resolve it. The fix is judged against a defined quality standard, such as all login tests passing with no regressions. Managing that task covers executing the fix, verifying it through tests, and measuring results such as error rates. Statement a gives the roles of tasks, capability and quality. Statement b gives the scope of task management. Neither makes task management exclusive of capability or quality, and neither denies anything the other states.

Example: the task 'launch a website' is the problem. A web-development team is the capability that resolves it, and the work is judged against load-time and accessibility targets (quality). Using decomposition as the method, it splits into subtasks such as 'design the layout' and 'build the backend'. Each subtask has its own intent (a usable UI; reliable data handling), its own capability (a designer; a backend engineer) and its own quality criteria (usability-test pass rate; uptime). This satisfies a's roles for task, capability and quality, and b's recursive decomposition. b adds 'intent' and recursion, which is extra detail rather than a conflict.

The statements address different things and can both hold. Statement a assigns roles: tasks are the problem, capability is the means, and quality is the standard the work is judged against. Statement b describes what happens when a task is decomposed and delegated. Example: a team is given the task of shipping a report (the problem). It uses its writing and analysis skills (capability) and is judged against an accuracy standard (quality). The team splits off a data-gathering subtask to a new sub-group. That sub-group inherits the shared language and communication channels, and adjusts its own check-in moments, deadlines (commitments) and exceptions. Every clause of both statements is satisfied.

Example: an agreement covers a set of tasks. Each task is a problem to solve, applied capability solves it, and the finished work is judged against a quality standard. Each task also has autonomy as one of its goals. Autonomy is not used as the yardstick for judging work, and it is not treated as the whole of the task. How far that autonomy extends is limited by the exceptions listed in the agreement. Statement a names quality as the standard, and statement b says autonomy is not a standard, so the two do not compete. A task that is a problem can still have goals.

Example: the task (the problem) is translating a contract. The capability used to resolve it is the translator's own fluency, which is intrinsic to the executor. The finished translation is judged against accuracy, which is the quality standard. This satisfies every clause of a. It also satisfies b, because the capability is intrinsic, and that holds whether b's 'or' is read as inclusive or exclusive. Statement a says nothing about where capability resides, so b's added detail does not conflict with it.

The two statements describe different things and do not conflict. Statement a assigns roles: tasks are the problem, capability is the means of resolving it, and quality is the standard the work is judged against. Statement b only says what intrinsic capability is made of: power, speed and context management. Example satisfying both: a translation job is the task. A system resolves it using capability, part of which is intrinsic capability made up of its power, speed and context management. The finished translation is judged against a quality standard such as accuracy. Every clause of a holds (task as problem, capability as means, quality as standard), and b holds because that intrinsic capability consists of power, speed and context management. Nothing in a limits what capability contains, and nothing in b assigns capability a different role.

The two statements describe different parts of one framework. (a) says what roles tasks, capability and quality play. (b) narrows one kind of capability, 'extrinsic', to know-how held outside the model. Nothing in (a) restricts what capability can consist of, so know-how can serve as a means. Example: an organisation must process supplier invoices (the task, i.e. the problem). An employee (the model) resolves it using the organisation's procedure manual, a training course and the applicable tax regulations. These are the extrinsic capability: know-how that belongs to the organisation, not the person. The work is judged against an accuracy and timeliness standard (quality). Every clause of both statements holds.

Both statements can hold in one framework. Example: a bridge-building firm. The task (spanning a river) is the problem. The firm's capability (engineering skill and equipment) is the means of solving it. Quality (load safety, durability) is the standard the finished work is judged against. That covers every clause of a. Separately, the firm's normative know-how, such as building codes and professional rules, adds no new capability. It limits which designs the firm may use, and it ties directly into the quality standards, since the codes set part of what counts as good work. That covers every clause of b. Statement a says nothing about normative know-how, so b's claim that it limits rather than extends capability does not conflict with a's view of capability as the means of resolution. Its link to quality also fits a's view of quality as the standard of judgment.

Example: a framework has three primitives. Tasks are the problem to solve. Capability is the means of solving it. Quality is the standard the work is judged against. Constraints, verification and monitoring are defined only as consequences of that quality standard: constraints state what quality requires, verification checks the work against it, and monitoring tracks it over time. None of the three is introduced as an independent primitive. Statement a says nothing about constraints, verification or monitoring, so b's added detail is consistent with it. Both statements hold in full.

Statement b only lists what quality consists of, while a says quality is the standard work is judged against. These fit together. Example: in a framework, the task is building a payment API (the problem) and the team's capability is the means of building it. The finished API is judged against quality, defined as fitness for purpose, verifiability, performance, security, resilience and maintainability. Every clause of a (task as problem, capability as means, quality as judging standard) and of b (the six quality attributes) holds at once.

Statement a assigns roles: tasks are the problem, capability is the means to resolve it, and quality is the standard the work is judged against. Statement b is a table of figures (form, fit, economy, completeness, order, sharpness, truthfulness). Each figure has an image and lists defects that count as slop, such as a term used before its definition or a claim of verification without evidence. Example satisfying both: a project with a task to fix a bug (the problem) and a programming capability used to fix it (the means). The resulting work is judged against a quality standard made up of b's seven figures, so b spells out what a's quality consists of. b says nothing that recasts tasks, capability or quality in conflicting roles. It only adds detail, which is not a contradiction.

Example: a framework holds that every task is a problem to solve, capability is how it gets solved, and quality is the standard the work is judged against. In it, the comparison loop is delegated to an agent under its own agreement. The agent runs the loop autonomously, using its capabilities, and at the end the user validates the result against the quality criteria. The loop is a task, so it fits a's framing. Its delegation, autonomy and end-of-loop user validation satisfy b. Nothing in a forbids delegation, autonomy or user validation, and nothing in b denies a's roles for task, capability and quality.

b is a question, so it asserts nothing and cannot conflict with a. Its only presupposition is that quality is either a property of the result or of the task–result relation. That can hold alongside a. Example: the task is translating a contract for a client (the problem). The translator's skill is the capability used to resolve it. Quality is the standard of fidelity to the client's brief, and the translation is judged against that standard. Here quality concerns the relation between task and result, and someone can still sensibly ask b. Every clause of a holds and b's presupposition is met.

Statement b is a question, so it asserts nothing that could clash with a. Example: a framework in which tasks are the problems, capability is the means of resolving them, and quality is the standard the work is judged against. Within that framework someone asks b and gets an answer: the measurement dimensions are cost, time and quality, and product quality (properties of the output) is separated from process quality (how the work was carried out). Every claim in a holds, and b is asked and answered without contradicting it.

Example: a team holds that communication runs through every working relationship and is far more than a channel. Its communication agreement has exactly six parts: shared language, chosen channels (e.g., chat and email), message format, meeting moments, response commitments, and rules for exceptions. Listing 'channels' as one of six components fits a's claim that communication is not only a channel. The agreement's other five components go beyond channels, and nothing in b denies that communication is the medium of every relation.

Both statements say communication underlies every relation, and neither limits or denies the other. Statement a calls communication the cross-cutting medium of every relation, more than a channel. Statement b says every relation is communication and classifies each relation by direction or mode. A concrete example satisfies both: a methodology in which distilling intent is downward communication, verifying or reporting a result is upward, consulting another is lateral, written know-how is communication deferred in time, and regulation is a judgement already made. Every relation is carried by communication, as a requires, and every relation is communication with the modes b's table gives. b's table is extra detail and does not conflict with a.

Statement a says what role communication plays: it is the medium of every relation. Statement b lists the properties each communication has. One model satisfies both. Every relation is carried by communications: person–agent, agent–agent and agent–environment. Each communication has a fidelity, a shared language, a direction, a timing and a recipient. Example: an agent's relation to a person is realized as a deferred, one-way note in English with high fidelity, addressed to that person. The agent's relation to its environment is an immediate signal addressed to the environment. Because every relation runs through such communications, communication is foundational and cross-cutting, not just one channel among others. Nothing in b limits communication to being a channel, so the two statements do not conflict.

Example: in an organization, every relation (assigning, reviewing, approving) is carried out through communication, so communication is more than a pipe. It is the medium of each relation, which satisfies a. When a lead splits a project and delegates a subtask to a new team, that team forms a new working group. It inherits the shared language and the existing chat and email channels, and it renegotiates its own meeting times, commitments and exception handling. That satisfies b. Calling channels part of the inherited base does not reduce communication to 'only a channel'. Both statements hold together.

The statements cover different things: (a) says when the agreement is settled, and (b) says what it contains. Example: a new working group's first act is to settle an agreement that specifies its working language, communication channels, document format, meeting moments, member commitments and how exceptions are handled. That agreement is the first thing settled and has exactly those six components, so every clause of both statements holds.

Example: a working group forms and its first act is to settle the agreement. Afterwards the group monitors and verifies the agreement on the same schedule as its other artefacts, and the agreement stays in force indefinitely, never lapsing however long it exists or however often it is used. Settling the agreement first does not stop it from being monitored later, and non-expiry concerns its duration, not its creation order, so every clause of both statements holds.

Example: a working group forms and the first thing it settles is the agreement. Later the agreement fails a verification, so it is reviewed. The review finds a defect, so the agreement is updated. Statement a only fixes the order at formation: the agreement is settled first. It does not say the agreement can never change afterward. So the later review-and-update process in b fits alongside it, and every clause of both statements holds.

Example: a team delegates a subtask, which creates a new subgroup (b). The subgroup's first act on forming is to settle its agreement (a). It does this by keeping the parent's language and channels and renegotiating its own moments, commitments and exceptions (b). Inheriting part of the agreement is still a way of settling it, so 'settles first' and 'inherited or renegotiated' hold together. Every clause of both statements is satisfied.

The two statements do not conflict. Example: a working group forms, and the first thing it settles is an agreement, which satisfies (a). That agreement lists exceptions, such as tasks that need sign-off before release. Each task aims at autonomy as its goal, not as a standard or as a property of the whole project, and the agreement's exceptions mark where that autonomy ends, which satisfies (b). Statement (a) says only when the agreement is settled. Statement (b) says what autonomy is and that the agreement's exceptions bound it. Neither requirement rules out the other.

The statements cover different things. (a) says when the agreement is settled: first, at the group's formation. (b) lists the possible responses to a diagnosis. Example satisfying both: a working group forms and settles its agreement before anything else. Later, a diagnosis is raised, and the available responses are exactly accept, accept with reservations, correct, escalate, or review the agreement or the intent. Reviewing the agreement later does not conflict with having settled it first.

Example: a working group forms, and the first thing it settles is its agreement (satisfies a). Later, an issue the agreement tolerates is resolved by the group at its own level, while an issue the agreement does not tolerate is escalated, so tolerability marks where the group's autonomy ends (satisfies b). Statement a fixes when the agreement is settled; b governs how issues are handled under it. Neither requires anything the other forbids, and reading 'its own level' as the group's or the issue's level gives the same answer.

These can both hold. Example: a working group forms and the first thing it settles is its agreement. Later it hands off the comparison loop as a delegated task. That task has its own separate agreement, runs autonomously internally, and the user validates the result at the end. Statement a only fixes when a working group settles its agreement. Statement b describes the comparison loop's own agreement and how it runs. Nothing requires a single agreement or forbids a delegated task from having one. Even if the comparison loop counts as a working group, its agreement can be the first thing it settles when it forms.

Example: an agreement made up of exactly six components (language, channels, format, moments, commitments and exceptions). Like every other artefact, it is regularly monitored and verified, and it has no expiry date or usage limit. Statement a only describes its structure. Statement b only describes how it is maintained and its lack of expiry. Nothing in the six components requires expiry, since 'moments' and 'exceptions' can be defined without ending the agreement, so both statements hold together.

Example: an agreement made up of exactly six components (language, channels, format, moments, commitments and exceptions) fails a verification. It is then reviewed, the review finds a defect, and the agreement is updated. Statement a describes the agreement's structure, while statement b sets conditional rules for review and update. Neither statement restricts the other, so both hold together.

The statements describe different things: a lists the six components of an agreement, and b lists five properties of a communication, so the differing counts do not clash. Example: a team's communication agreement has exactly six sections (language: English; channels: chat and email; format: bullet summaries; moments: daily standup; commitments: reply within 24h; exceptions: emergencies by phone). Separately, one message sent under it has fidelity: high, shared language: English, direction: one-way, timing: deferred, and recipient: a person. Every clause of both statements holds.

Both can hold in one example. Take an agreement with six components: language, channels, format, moments, commitments and exceptions. When a task is decomposed and delegated, the new working group inherits language and channels unchanged and adjusts moments, commitments and exceptions. Format, which b does not mention, is also inherited. That satisfies a's six-component list and every clause of b. Leaving format out of b is silence, not a claim that the agreement has only five parts.

Example: an agreement has exactly six components: language, channels, format, moments, commitments and exceptions. Its exceptions component lists the cases where autonomy stops (e.g., budget overruns require escalation), which sets autonomy's boundary. Separately, each task treats autonomy as a goal, not as a standard or as a whole. Statement b relies on the agreement having exceptions, which statement a supplies. Nothing in b adds a seventh component or conflicts with the six-part structure.

The two statements describe different things: a lists the six components of the agreement, and b lists the possible responses to a diagnosis. Neither sets a count or limit for the other. Concrete example: a framework defines its agreement as having exactly language, channels, format, moments, commitments and exceptions. In the same framework, a diagnosis can be met only by accept, accept with reservations, correct, escalate, or review the agreement or the intent. b's option to review the agreement fits a, which defines what that agreement contains. Every clause of both statements holds.

Statement a lists what the agreement contains. Statement b describes how issues under it are handled. Neither limits the other. Example: an agreement made of exactly six components (language, channels, format, moments, commitments, exceptions). Deviations that stay within tolerable limits are settled by the agreement's parties themselves, and intolerable ones are escalated. That handling rule could sit inside the 'exceptions' component, so no seventh component is needed. Tolerability marks how far the parties' autonomy extends. Every clause of both statements holds.

The two statements describe different things. Statement a says the agreement has six components: language, channels, format, moments, commitments and exceptions. Statement b is a table of seven quality figures (form, fit, economy, completeness, order, sharpness, truthfulness), each paired with an image and the kinds of slop it covers in this work. It does not list or count the agreement's components. Concrete example: a work contains an agreement with exactly those six components, and a separate quality rubric uses the seven-row table to classify defects, e.g. 'a term used before its definition' falls under 'order'. Both statements hold in full. The different counts (six components vs. seven figures) are not a conflict because b never claims its rows are the agreement's components.

Nothing conflicts. Example: the main agreement has exactly six components: language, channels, format, moments, commitments and exceptions. The comparison loop is a delegated task with its own separate agreement. That agreement could even use the same six components, e.g. moments = the user validates only at the end, and commitments = the loop runs autonomously inside. The loop runs on its own and the user validates the result at the end. Statement a counts the parts of an agreement; b says a task has its own agreement and how it operates. Neither limits the other.

Example: in a methodology where every relation is communication, a written agreement is treated as an artefact. A reviewer verifies it and reports the result upward, which is the same upward communication used for any other artefact. The agreement then stays in force indefinitely, regardless of time elapsed or how often it is invoked. Statement a classifies relations as kinds of communication and says nothing about how artefacts are monitored or how long they last. Statement b's verification fits a's 'verifying or reporting a result' row, and its non-expiry touches nothing in a. Every clause of both statements holds.

The two statements fit together. Statement a classifies every relation of the methodology as communication. Statement b describes a conditional process: a failed verification triggers a review, and a defect found in review triggers an update. Example: a result is checked against the agreement and fails. That failure is reported upward, which a calls upward communication. The review is done by consulting a peer, which a calls lateral communication. The reviewer finds a defect, and the written agreement is updated; that update can be treated as deferred communication or as a judgement already made. Every relation in this sequence is communication, and both of b's conditions are met. Nothing in a forbids reviewing or updating agreements.

Statement a classifies every relation of the methodology as a kind of communication. Statement b lists the properties any communication has. Nothing in one rules out the other. Example model satisfying both: (1) Distilling intent: lead to agent; direction downward, timing immediate, recipient agent, shared language English, fidelity high. (2) Verifying a result: agent reports to lead; direction upward, timing immediate, recipient person. (3) Consulting another: peer to peer; direction lateral, timing immediate, recipient person. (4) Written know-how: a document read later; direction downward, timing deferred, recipient agent. (5) Regulation: a prior judgement encoded as a rule; direction downward, timing deferred, recipient environment or person. Each relation is a communication, as a requires, and each carries fidelity, shared language, direction, timing and recipient, as b requires.

Example: a three-level organisation. The top level sets its intent and distils it downward to the middle level. The middle level sets its own intent from that and distils it downward to the bottom level, which sets its own intent in turn. Results are reported upward, peers consult laterally, written know-how is passed on later in time, and regulations stand as judgements already made. Every relation is communication, as a requires, and intent is set at each level, as b requires. Downward distillation of intent does not stop each level from setting its own intent; it describes how one level's intent informs the next.

Concrete example: a three-level project. The director tells the team lead, 'ship a usable beta by June.' That is downward communication, distilling intent. The lead does not just copy this. The lead forms a complementary intent that serves it: 'stabilise the login and payment flows first.' A developer then forms 'fix the session-timeout bug this week' to fulfil the lead's intent. So intent passes down non-strictly, with each level complementing and fulfilling the one above, as b requires. Every relation in the methodology is still communication, as a requires. Results are reported upward, developers consult peers laterally, and the team follows a written runbook (deferred communication) and a security regulation (a judgement already made). B's inheritance of intent is carried by a's downward 'distilling intent' relation, so it adds no relation that is not communication. Nothing in either statement conflicts.

Statement a classes distilling intent as downward communication. Statement b says intent is distilled from level to level. These fit together. Example: a director distils intent to a manager, and the manager distils it to a team lead. That is downward communication passing level to level. In the same methodology, the team lead reports results upward, consults peers laterally, follows written know-how (communication deferred in time) and obeys regulations (judgements already made). So every relation is communication, as a requires, and b is satisfied.

The two statements describe verification from different angles. Statement a says the verifying or reporting relation counts as upward communication. Statement b says what verification checks. Concrete example: a developer sends a test report up to the team lead (upward communication, satisfying a). The lead confirms the result meets the team-level intent and that this intent still serves the project-level goal (satisfying b). The other rows of a's table (downward distilling, lateral consulting, deferred written know-how, regulation as a prior judgement) can all hold alongside this. Nothing in b requires verification to be anything other than communication.

Statement a classifies every relation of the methodology as a form of communication: distilling intent goes downward, verifying or reporting a result goes upward, consulting another is lateral, written know-how is deferred in time, and regulation is a judgement already made. Statement b says only that drift can empty the original intent of meaning. Neither constrains the other. Concrete example: a founder distils an intent ('ship only what users can understand') down to teams, which is downward communication. Teams report results upward and consult each other laterally. The intent is written into a handbook (deferred communication) and later frozen into a rule (a judgement already made). Years on, staff follow the rule mechanically, and its wording has drifted so far that it no longer carries the founder's purpose. Every relation is still communication, satisfying a, and drift has emptied the original intent of meaning, satisfying b. Statement a never claims that communication preserves meaning or rules out drift.

The two statements address different things. Statement a says every relation in the methodology is a form of communication: distilling intent goes downward, verifying or reporting a result goes upward, consulting is lateral, written know-how is deferred in time, and regulation is a judgement already made. Statement b says that managing tasks covers execution, verification and measurement. Example satisfying both: a methodology whose task management includes doing the work, checking it and measuring it. In that methodology, verification is reported upward as communication. Execution and measurement are activities rather than relations, and any relations they involve, such as reporting measurements upward, are also communication. Nothing in a prohibits task management from covering these activities, and nothing in b requires a relation that is not communication.

Example: the methodology is decomposition. 'Launch product' splits into 'build' and 'market', and 'build' splits into 'backend' and 'frontend'. Each task at every level has its own intent, capability and quality bar, which satisfies b's recursion. Every relation in the methodology is communication, which satisfies a: the parent distils intent downward to each subtask, subtasks verify and report results upward, sibling tasks consult laterally, written know-how carries guidance across time, and regulation applies judgements already made. b calls decomposition the methodology itself, not a relation within it, so it adds nothing outside a's list. Even if the parent-to-subtask link counted as a relation, it is downward communication of intent. Both statements hold together.

Example: an organisation's methodology has five relations, each treated as communication. Managers distil intent downward to a model, the person. The model reports and verifies results upward and consults peers laterally. A procedure manual the organisation wrote last year reaches the model as communication deferred in time. A safety regulation the organisation adopted reaches it as a judgement already made. That satisfies a. The manual, a training course and the regulation are the model's extrinsic capability. They count as know-how and belong to the organisation, not the person. That satisfies b. Statement a's table gives regulation its own row, but it only says how each relation works as communication. It does not say the rows exclude one another, so a regulation can be organisational know-how and also a judgement already made.

A concrete case fits both. A methodology has a written regulation stating what must not be done. Under b it is normative written know-how. Under a it is communication in two ways: as written know-how it is deferred in time, and as regulation it is a judgement already made. These descriptions do not conflict, because a judgement made earlier and read later is also communication deferred in time. The table in a does not say its rows exclude each other. b's three kinds of written know-how (descriptive, procedural, normative) add detail and require nothing that a forbids. The other relations (downward, upward, lateral) are unaffected.

Statement a only says that every relation in the methodology is a form of communication, and it classes written know-how as communication deferred in time and regulation as a judgement already made. Statement b says that normative know-how restricts capability rather than extending it, and that it ties directly to quality. Classifying know-how as communication says nothing about whether it extends or limits capability, so the two do not clash. Concrete example: a team's written coding standard is communication deferred in time, and as a rule it is also a judgement already made. It forbids certain constructs, which limits what developers may do, and it exists to ensure code quality. Every other relation in the team's methodology is also communication: managers hand intent down, developers report results up, and peers consult each other laterally. This satisfies every clause of both statements.

Example: in a methodology, distilling intent is downward communication, verifying or reporting a result is upward, consulting a colleague is lateral, written know-how (a manual) is communication deferred in time, and regulation is a judgement already made. Embodied know-how, a skill held in a practitioner's head, is reached by consulting that practitioner, which is the lateral 'consulting another' relation. Statement a gives no row for embodied know-how and does not say the table is exhaustive. Even if it were exhaustive, b places embodied know-how inside an existing row, so it remains communication. Separating it from written know-how ('deferred in time') does not conflict with a.

Both can hold in one example. A team's methodology works like this: a lead distils intent and passes it down to an executor, the executor reports results up, and peers consult each other laterally. Regulations record judgements already made. Know-how is written in a shared runbook stored outside any executor, which makes it communication deferred in time, as A says. As B requires, each executor must retrieve the runbook to use it. It is updated with lessons learned, and a replacement executor reuses it unchanged. Every relation is still communication, and B's claims about external, retrievable, growing, reusable know-how fit A's 'deferred in time' framing of written know-how.

Example: a team's methodology treats every relation as communication. Distilling intent flows downward, verifying or reporting results flows upward, consulting peers is lateral, regulation is a judgement already made, and written know-how is a message deferred in time to future readers. Because the team's environment keeps changing, it adds new written notes over time, reviews them periodically, and retires notes that are no longer valid. Treating know-how as deferred communication does not stop it from being accumulated, reviewed or retired, and b does not deny that know-how is communication. Both statements hold.

The two statements answer different questions. a says what form every relation takes: each one is communication. b says where constraints, verification and monitoring come from: they derive from quality, and none is a starting point of its own. Concrete example: a methodology starts from quality goals. From those goals it derives constraints, written as regulation, which a lists as 'a judgement already made'. It also derives verification, carried out as upward reporting of results, and monitoring, carried out as ongoing upward or lateral communication. Every relation, including distilling intent, consulting and written know-how, is still a form of communication. Each item is derived from quality, so none is a starting point, and nothing in a names communication or anything else as the methodology's starting point.

Statement a classes verifying or reporting a result as upward communication. Statement b says what a verification returns: a diagnosis rather than a bare yes or no. These are about different things, the direction of the communication and the content of the result, and do not conflict. Example: within the methodology, intent is distilled downward, peers are consulted laterally, know-how is written down, and regulations record judgements already made. A reviewer verifies a delivered module and reports upward to whoever commissioned it: 'The parser fails on empty input because the length check runs after indexing; the other cases pass.' That report is upward communication, so it satisfies a, and it is a diagnosis rather than a yes or no, so it satisfies b.

The statements cover different things. A says every relation in the methodology is a form of communication, as its table lists. B gives the closed set of responses to a diagnosis. Nothing in either rules out the other. Example: in a methodology, a lead distils intent downward to a worker. The worker reports a diagnosis upward, consults a peer laterally, draws on written know-how (communication deferred in time) and follows regulation (a judgement already made). Every relation is therefore communication. The lead's only options on receiving the diagnosis are to accept it, accept it with reservations, correct it, escalate it, or review the agreement or the intent. Each response is itself communication, for example escalation goes upward. Both statements hold in full.

The two statements cover different subjects. Statement a says every relation in the methodology is communication: distilling intent is downward, verifying or reporting a result is upward, consulting another is lateral, written know-how is deferred in time, and regulation is a judgement already made. Statement b is a table of seven figures (form, fit, economy, completeness, order, sharpness, truthfulness), each with an image and the kind of 'slop' it names in this work. Neither table limits the other. Concrete example: a methodology where a lead passes intent downward to a worker, the worker reports verified results upward, peers consult laterally, guides record know-how for later readers, and regulations stand as judgements already made, so every relation is communication. The same methodology classifies defects in its texts using b's table, for example a term with two meanings as a form failure, the same thing said twice as an economy failure, and a claim of verification without evidence as a truthfulness failure. Both statements hold in full. Statement b defines what counts as slop; it does not claim that a's table is free of slop, so even an undefined term in a would not make the two statements contradict each other.

One methodology can satisfy both statements. Take one where intent is distilled downward, results are verified or reported upward, consultation is lateral, know-how is written down, and regulation is a recorded prior judgement. That makes every relation communication, as in a. Requirements are also written in a decidable description logic such as OWL DL. In that logic, each minimal unsatisfiable subset counts as one contradiction, and an element the others entail counts as redundant.
