It then asks which dimensions are measured and how product quality differs from process quality, for instance by measuring the output's defects separately from the workflow's repeatability. Both texts hold together.

Example: a team delegates a subtask to a new subgroup. The subgroup inherits the base (same language and channels) and adjusts its local parts: its own meeting moments, commitments and exceptions. That satisfies (a). For this subtask, autonomy is one of the task's goals. It is not a uniform standard or a whole, and its limits are whatever the subgroup's locally adjusted exceptions specify. That satisfies (b). Because exceptions are renegotiated at each level, autonomy boundaries can differ from task to task, which fits (b)'s claim that autonomy is not a standard. Every clause of both statements holds together.

The statements cover different matters: (a) how agreements carry over when a task is decomposed and delegated, and (b) the set of allowed responses to a diagnosis. Nothing in either limits the other. Concrete example: a project team splits its work and delegates a module to a new subgroup. The subgroup inherits the shared language and communication channels and adjusts its own meeting times, commitments and exceptions. Later, someone issues a diagnosis about the subgroup's progress. The subgroup's available responses are exactly: accept, accept with reservations, correct, escalate, or review the agreement or the intent. For instance, it chooses to review its local agreement. Every clause of both statements holds in this scenario.

The two statements address different aspects and can both hold. Example: a project team delegates a subtask to a new subgroup. The subgroup inherits the team's language and channels (a's base) and sets its own meeting moments, commitments and exceptions (a's local parts). Later, a minor delay that stays within the subgroup's agreement is handled by the subgroup itself. A breach beyond what the agreement tolerates is escalated to the parent team (b). So a covers how each level's agreement is formed, and b covers which issues are resolved at that level versus escalated. Nothing in a forbids escalation, and nothing in b forbids inheriting or adjusting agreements.

The two statements cover different subjects and share no requirement that could clash. (a) says that decomposing and delegating a task creates a new working group: base elements (language, channels) are inherited, and local elements (moments, commitments, exceptions) are adjusted at each level. (b) is a table of quality figures (form, fit, economy, completeness, order, sharpness, truthfulness), each with an image and the kinds of slop it names in this work. Concrete example: a project delegates a subtask to a subgroup. The subgroup inherits the project's language and channels and renegotiates its own meeting moments, commitments and exceptions. The same project judges its documents with b's table: it flags terms with two meanings, elements in the wrong language, contradictory or untraceable elements, repetition, undefined terms or unverified tasks, terms used before their definition, ambiguous sentences, and verification claims without evidence. Every clause of a and b holds in this example. b says nothing about how delegation works, and a says nothing about what counts as slop.

Example: a user delegates a comparison loop to a sub-team, which forms a new working group as statement a describes. The loop's agreement keeps the parent's language and channels, so the base is inherited. Its local parts are adjusted: the team works autonomously inside the loop (commitments and exceptions), and the user validates the result at the end (moments). That gives the loop 'its own agreement' as statement b says, while matching a's inherit-the-base, adjust-the-local-parts structure. 'Its own' does not require a base unrelated to the parent's, so both statements hold.

Statement b is a question and asserts nothing, so it adds no requirement that could clash with a. Concrete example: a project lead splits a report into sections and delegates one to a subteam. This forms a new working group. It inherits the shared base (English, the team Slack channel) and adjusts local parts (its own check-in times, a section deadline commitment, an exception allowing late data). That satisfies every clause of a. In that same situation someone can coherently ask whether the section's quality lies in the result itself or in how well it fits the delegated task. Raising that question requires nothing that a rules out.

The statements cover different subjects and share no requirement that could clash. Statement a defines autonomy as a per-task goal, not a standard or a whole, bounded by the agreement's exceptions. Statement b lists five possible responses to a diagnosis. Concrete example: a working agreement under which each task aims at autonomy, and that autonomy extends only up to the exceptions written into the agreement. When a diagnosis is issued, the recipient may accept it, accept it with reservations, correct it, escalate it, or review the agreement or the intent. Every clause of both statements holds in this arrangement.

Example: a team's service agreement lists exceptions, such as any cost overrun above 10% or any safety incident. Every task aims for the team to handle it independently, so autonomy is a goal of each task rather than a standard or a whole. Issues outside the listed exceptions count as tolerable and are resolved at team level. Issues that hit an exception are not tolerable and are escalated. The exceptions set the boundary of autonomy (statement a), and that same line is the tolerable/intolerable line that marks the boundary (statement b). 'Set by' and 'marks' fit together when the exceptions define what is tolerable, so every clause of both statements holds.

The two statements cover different topics and neither restricts the other. Statement a describes autonomy as a goal of each task, not a standard, with its limit set by the agreement's exceptions. Statement b is a table that classifies kinds of 'slop' in the work under seven figures (form, fit, economy, completeness, order, sharpness, truthfulness). Concrete example: a project agreement says each task aims at autonomy except where the agreement lists exceptions (e.g., 'deployment requires sign-off'). Autonomy is not listed as one of the quality standards. The same work treats as slop exactly the table's items, such as a term used before it is defined, a task without verification, or a claim of verification without evidence. Nothing in b makes autonomy a standard or a whole, or changes how its boundary is set. Nothing in a conflicts with any figure in b. Both hold at once.

Example: the comparison loop is one task with its own agreement. Autonomy is that task's goal. The agreement contains one exception: the user validates the result at the end. Inside the loop the task runs autonomously, and its autonomy stops at that validation. This satisfies a: autonomy is a goal of this task, is not total, and its boundary is set by the agreement's exception. It also satisfies b: the loop is a delegated task with its own agreement, autonomous inside and validated by the user at the end. b's limited autonomy fits a's statement that autonomy is not a whole.

No conflict is possible because b is a question and asserts nothing. It is also about quality, while a is about autonomy. Concrete example: under a service agreement, each task has autonomy as one of its goals, not as a standard or an overall whole. The agreement's listed exceptions mark where that autonomy stops. In the same setting someone asks whether quality belongs to the result or to the task–result relation. Every clause of a holds, and asking b's question is consistent with either answer.

Statement b is a question, so it asserts nothing that could conflict with a. Even if b is read as the claim that more verifiable results can be delegated more, both can hold. Example: in an agreement, autonomy is a goal pursued separately for each task, not a general standard or a single whole. The agreement's exceptions mark its limits, and those exceptions are drawn by verifiability. Tasks with easily checked results (e.g., a computation with a test suite) carry no exception and are fully delegated. Hard-to-verify tasks (e.g., judgment calls) are listed as exceptions requiring sign-off. The boundary is set by the exceptions, as a requires, and delegability rises with verifiability, as b's reading requires.

Example: an executor's capabilities divide into intrinsic ones (its own power, speed and context management) and extrinsic ones (e.g., external tools it is given). Every capability is intrinsic or extrinsic, which satisfies a, and the intrinsic category is exactly power, speed and context management, which satisfies b. Statement b only details what the intrinsic category contains and does not conflict with a's classification, whether a's 'or' is read as inclusive or exclusive.

Example: a person (the model/executor) has an intrinsic capability, such as their own trained skill. The organisation's documents, courses and regulations are an extrinsic capability, and that capability is know-how. Each capability is either intrinsic or extrinsic, so (a) holds. The extrinsic capability is know-how belonging to the organisation, matching (b)'s claim and analogy. Statement (b) only characterises the extrinsic category and does not conflict with (a)'s division.

The two statements address different things, so both can hold at once. Statement a only classifies capability as either intrinsic or extrinsic to the executor; this holds whether the 'or' is read inclusively or exclusively. Statement b says normative know-how restricts capability rather than extending it, and is directly tied to quality. Example: a craftsman's capability is intrinsic (his own skill), which satisfies a. The trade's normative standards narrow what he may do with that skill and add no new capability; they bear directly on the quality of his work, which satisfies b. Nothing in a rules out capability being limited, so no clause conflicts.

Statement a is only a disjunction: capability is either intrinsic or extrinsic to the executor. Statement b places know-how outside the executor, which fits the extrinsic option. Concrete example: an agent whose skills are stored in an external skill library. The agent retrieves a skill when it needs one, the library gains new entries as the agent learns, and the same library is reused when the agent's underlying model is swapped. Here capability is extrinsic, so a holds, and every clause of b holds. This also works on the reading that a classifies each capability as exactly one of the two, because this capability is extrinsic and not intrinsic.

The two statements define different concepts, so nothing conflicts. Statement a defines intrinsic capability as power, speed and context management. Statement b defines extrinsic capability as know-how. Its analogy casts the person as the model, and the organisation's documents, courses and regulations as the know-how. Concrete example: an AI framework that classifies a model's raw power, speed and context handling as intrinsic capability, and the organisation's procedures, training material and rules as extrinsic know-how owned by the organisation. This satisfies every clause of both statements.

Example: intrinsic capability consists of exactly power, speed and context management. Normative know-how is a separate factor. It adds nothing to that capability, constrains how it can be used, and directly affects output quality. This satisfies a's list of components and every clause of b: it does not extend capability, it limits it, and it connects with quality. Normative know-how is not among a's components, which fits b's claim that it does not extend capability.

Example: an organisation owns its documentation and glossary (descriptive), its courses and methods (procedural) and its regulations (normative). These written materials are its know-how, which is its extrinsic capability. Its staff stand in the 'model' role of the analogy. Statement a says documents, courses and regulations are know-how belonging to the organisation, and statement b sorts written know-how into exactly those three kinds. b adds a classification without conflicting with anything in a.

The answer depends on what 'capability' means in b. Reading 1 (compatible): b's 'capability' means the person's (the model's) overall capability. Statement a treats regulations as organisational know-how, which counts as extrinsic capability. Statement b adds that this normative kind of know-how limits what the person can do and is tied to quality. Example: an organisation's documents and courses broaden what staff can do, while its regulations restrict how they act in order to secure quality. Both statements hold. Reading 2 (contradiction): a equates extrinsic capability with know-how, so any added know-how, regulations included, adds extrinsic capability by definition. Then normative know-how does extend capability, which directly conflicts with b's claim that it 'does not extend capability; it limits it.' The pair does not settle which sense of 'capability' b uses.

Example: a framework defines extrinsic capability as know-how held outside the model. In the analogy, a person is the model, and the organisation owns its documents, courses and regulations. Within that know-how there is a category called 'embodied know-how': the know-how carried by another person, such as a colleague, which the model accesses by consulting them. That satisfies (a), which defines extrinsic capability as know-how and gives the organisational analogy, and (b), which says embodied know-how is consulting another. Know-how embodied in someone else is still extrinsic to the model, so nothing clashes. Statement (a) does not say documents are the only form of know-how, so (b) adds detail rather than contradicting it.

Example: a company keeps its procedures, training courses and regulations in a shared repository that the company owns. That know-how is the extrinsic capability, matching statement a, where the employee or model is the executor and the documents belong to the organisation. It sits outside the executor, so the employee must look it up (retrieved). The company adds lessons learned to the repository (grows). When the employee is replaced by someone else, or a model is swapped, the new executor uses the same documents (reused). Statement a defines know-how as external and organisationally owned. Statement b draws consequences from that externality. Every clause of both holds in this one scenario.

The two statements fit together. A defines extrinsic capability as know-how: documents, courses and regulations that belong to the organisation rather than to the person (the model). B describes how that know-how changes over time: it is accumulated, reviewed, and retired once it is no longer valid. Example: a company keeps a library of procedures, training courses and compliance rules. Its staff use this library, but the company owns it. The library grows as new procedures are added, is reviewed periodically, and drops a regulation when that regulation is repealed. Every clause of both statements holds in this case.

Statement a sorts written know-how into three types: descriptive, procedural and normative. Statement b adds claims about the normative type only, and nothing in a contradicts them. Example: a firm's written know-how consists of product documentation and a glossary (descriptive), training courses and work methods (procedural), and a quality regulation stating what staff must and must not do (normative). The regulation teaches no new skills, so it does not extend capability. It forbids certain shortcuts, so it limits capability. It is written directly to meet the firm's quality standards. Every clause of both statements holds.

The statements describe different categories: (a) classifies written know-how into three types, and (b) defines embodied know-how. Example: in an organization's knowledge model, written know-how takes three forms: the documentation and glossary (descriptive), courses and methods (procedural), and regulations (normative). Embodied know-how is accessed by consulting a colleague. Every clause of both statements holds, and nothing in (a) says written know-how is the only kind.

Statement a sorts written know-how into three kinds. Statement b says know-how is external to the executor, so it must be retrieved, it can grow, and it can be reused. These do not clash. Example: a team keeps a glossary and documentation (descriptive), a methods guide and courses (procedural), and a regulation (normative) in a shared wiki outside any single worker. A worker retrieves these documents when doing a task. After a lesson is learned, the methods guide is updated, so the know-how grows. When that worker is replaced, the new worker reuses the same documents. Every clause of a and every clause of b holds in this example.

Statement a sorts written know-how into three types: descriptive, procedural and normative. Statement b says know-how has a lifecycle: it is accumulated, reviewed and retired when no longer valid. One can be a taxonomy and the other a lifecycle without conflict. Example: a team's glossary entry (descriptive), its onboarding course (procedural) and a regulation on data handling (normative) are each added over time and periodically reviewed. When the regulation is superseded, it is retired. Every piece is written know-how of one of the three types, and all of it follows the accumulate/review/retire cycle in a changing environment.

Example: an organisation's written know-how is its documentation and glossary (descriptive), a training course (procedural) and a regulation (normative), matching a's three categories. All definitions sit in the glossary and nowhere else; the course and regulation only use the terms. Glossary entry 1: 'Widget: a small metal part used in assembly' (plain language, no defined terms). Entry 2: 'Widget tray: a container that holds widgets' (uses only 'widget', defined earlier, not its own term). This satisfies b's placement, ordering and non-circularity rules. Statement a only classifies kinds of know-how and says the glossary is descriptive, which b's definitions-only glossary fits. This treats b's 'terms' as glossary terms, not every ordinary word, so the first entry can be written in plain language.

The two statements describe different things. (a) is about normative know-how and (b) is about embodied know-how, and neither says anything about the other kind. Example satisfying every clause: In a workshop, normative know-how is the set of rules about what counts as acceptable work. Those rules add no new abilities, they restrict what a worker may do, and they are tied directly to the quality of the product. Separately, embodied know-how in that workshop consists of consulting another person, such as asking an experienced colleague how to do a task. Every clause of (a) and (b) holds in this scenario.

Example: a team's coding-standards guide is kept in a shared repository, not inside the AI agent that writes code. The guide only constrains what the agent may produce, such as banned patterns and required tests, so it limits capability rather than extending it, and it directly governs output quality. That satisfies a. The agent must retrieve the guide before working. New rules are added as lessons are learned, so the guide grows while still only restricting the agent. When the agent is replaced by a different model, the same guide is reused. That satisfies b. Growth in know-how is not the same as extending capability, so the two statements do not clash.

Example: a team keeps a set of normative rules, such as 'never deploy without passing the regression suite.' These rules add no new abilities. They restrict what may be done and exist to protect output quality, which satisfies a. Because tools and conditions keep changing, the team adds new rules over time, reviews them periodically, and retires a rule once it no longer applies, such as one tied to a decommissioned server. That satisfies b. Statement a describes what normative know-how does, and statement b describes how know-how is managed over time. Both clauses hold together.

Example: in a quality-management framework, quality requirements are the sole origin. Constraints, verification steps and monitoring are each derived from those requirements, so none is a starting point of its own (b). The framework's normative know-how, meaning knowledge of what one may or may not do, adds no new capability. It only restricts what practitioners may do, and it is tied directly to the quality requirements (a). Whether or not normative know-how counts as a kind of constraint, being derived from quality is consistent with connecting directly with it, so every clause of both statements holds.

The two statements address different subjects and impose no conflicting requirements. Example: a team's normative know-how is its coding standards and security policies. These do not add new capabilities; they restrict which designs and practices are allowed, so they limit capability. The restrictions directly shape the product's quality. That quality is defined by fitness for purpose, verifiability, performance, security, resilience and maintainability. Statement a holds (know-how limits rather than extends capability and connects directly with quality), and statement b holds (quality has the six listed attributes). Nothing in b says what extends or limits capability, and nothing in a defines quality's attributes.

Statement b is a question, not an assertion, so it adds no requirement that could clash with a. Example: in a craft workshop, knowing the norms of good joinery stops a carpenter from making certain cuts he could otherwise make. That limits his capability rather than extending it, and it bears directly on the quality of the work. This satisfies every clause of a. Someone can still sensibly ask b, whether that quality belongs to the finished joint itself or to how well the joint fits the task, and either answer is consistent with a.

Statement b is a question. It asserts nothing, but it presupposes that measurement has dimensions and that product quality can be separated from process quality. Statement a only claims that normative know-how limits capability rather than extending it, and that it connects with quality. Concrete example: in a factory, standard operating rules (normative know-how) restrict what workers may do and are tied to quality outcomes. Quality is measured along dimensions such as defect rate and cycle time, and product quality (finished-item defects) is assessed separately from process quality (adherence and variability of steps). Every clause of a holds, and b's presuppositions are satisfied.

Statement a is unclear, and the answer depends on how it is read. Read literally, 'embodied know-how consists in consulting another (agent or source)' puts the know-how outside the executor. That fits b. Example: a robot whose skills are stored in an external library. It must retrieve them, the library grows as the robot learns, and a replacement robot can reuse it. Read as shorthand for 'embodied know-how is one thing; consulting another is a different thing', a asserts know-how held inside the executor. Then the result depends on b's scope. If b is a universal claim that all know-how lives outside the executor, it cannot also be held inside, so the two conflict. If b describes only one system or one kind of know-how, they are compatible. Neither reading clearly wins.

Example: in a workshop, embodied know-how takes the form of a worker consulting another, experienced colleague, which satisfies a. Because the workshop's conditions keep changing, the crew builds up such practices, periodically reviews them, and drops any that no longer work, which satisfies b. Nothing in a forbids know-how from being accumulated, reviewed or retired, and b does not exclude it being embodied or involving consultation.

Example: an AI agent (the executor) pulls know-how from an external knowledge base, so it must retrieve it. The base keeps adding lessons learned (it grows, i.e. is accumulated). Entries are reviewed periodically, and entries invalidated by a changing environment are retired. When the agent is swapped for a new model, the same base is reused. This satisfies every clause of a (external location, retrieval, growth, reuse across executor changes) and every clause of b (living environment; accumulation, review and retirement of invalid know-how). Growth and retirement can coexist, since adding new entries does not forbid removing stale ones.

The two statements cover different things and can both hold. Example: a team keeps a knowledge base. Each entry is added, reviewed periodically, and retired once it no longer applies, which satisfies a. Separately, whenever a diagnosis is produced, the team responds in exactly one of the listed ways: accept, accept with reservations, correct, escalate, or review the agreement or the intent, which satisfies b. Retiring knowledge is part of managing the knowledge base, not a response to a diagnosis, so b's closed list of responses is not broken.

Both can hold in one framework. Example: a quality model defines quality by exactly these six attributes: fitness for purpose, verifiability, performance, security, resilience and maintainability. In that model, constraints are derived from the security and performance requirements. Verification activities are derived from the verifiability attribute. Monitoring is derived from the resilience and performance attributes. None of the three is treated as an independent starting point; each traces back to quality. Statement b only lists what quality consists of and says nothing about where constraints, verification or monitoring originate. Naming verifiability as an attribute of quality is consistent with verification deriving from quality.

Example: a team defines the quality goal 'pages load within 200 ms.' From that goal it derives a constraint (no uncached database calls on the render path), a verification (a load test), and monitoring (latency dashboards). None of these exists independently of the goal, which satisfies a. When the load test runs, it reports 'median 340 ms; the delay comes from an uncached user-profile query' rather than pass or fail, which satisfies b. Statement a concerns where verification comes from, and b concerns what it outputs. Neither restricts the other.

Both can hold in one framework: quality is the only root, broken into b's seven figures. Constraints, verification and monitoring are derived from those figures, and none stands as an independent starting point. For example, the requirement to verify a task follows from 'completeness' (a task without verification is a hole), and honest verification claims follow from 'truthfulness'. Table b only lists quality figures, their images and slop examples. It never makes constraints, verification or monitoring a starting point of its own; its mentions of verification are already framed as quality defects, which fits a's claim that verification derives from quality.

A concrete scenario satisfies both. Quality is the root, and constraints, verification and monitoring are each derived from it. The derived elements are written as description-logic formulas, which are decidable. A contradiction is then any minimal unsatisfiable subset, and an element is redundant when the remaining formulas entail it. The consistency and redundancy judgement is made once at formalisation and recorded, so verification no longer carries it. Statement b never makes constraints, verification or monitoring a starting point. Moving a judgement from verification to formalisation does not stop verification deriving from quality. Statement a does not cover formalisation, so even treating formalisation as independent would not conflict with it.

The two statements address different questions. Statement a says where constraints, verification and monitoring come from: they all derive from quality, and none is a starting point of its own. Statement b describes how one verification step, judging contradiction, works until a logic is chosen. That step uses model anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 at temperature 0 with the template identified by its SHA-256 hash. Each pair that shares a term is sent alone. A reply is contradiction (naming the conflicting requirements), compatible (with an example) or refer. A refer goes to the user. A schema failure or transport failure leaves the verification incomplete and is not a decision. Statement b never says verification is a starting point or independent of quality. Concrete example: a framework defines quality as its sole root concept. Constraints, verification and monitoring are each defined as consequences of quality requirements. The contradiction check inside that derived verification runs exactly as b specifies. Every clause of both statements holds.

Statement a says where verification comes from: it derives from quality and is not a starting point. Statement b says how verification runs: judgements are cached by hash and only redone when a hash changes. Neither claim limits the other. Example: a project first defines its quality criteria. From those criteria it derives its constraints, its monitoring, and a verification step. That verification step records each judgement with the input hash, the template hash, the models, N and k. On a later run it reads the record and judges again only if the input or template hash has changed. Every clause of both statements holds.

Statement b is a question, so it asserts nothing that could clash with a. At most it presupposes that quality is a property of something, either of the result or of the task–result relation. Example satisfying both: quality is defined as the fit between a task and its result. Constraints, verification and monitoring are all derived from that quality definition, and none is treated as an independent starting point. Choosing the other answer, that quality is a property of the result alone, is equally consistent with a.

Statement b is a question, so it asserts nothing. Its only presuppositions are that measurement has dimensions and that product quality can be distinguished from process quality. A concrete case meets everything. Take a framework where quality is the sole root concept, and constraints, verification and monitoring are each defined from it, none standing alone. Measurement has dimensions such as accuracy, completeness and timeliness. Product quality is judged on the output, process quality on how the output is produced. Nothing in a rules out measurement dimensions or the product/process split, so both hold together.

Statement b is a question, not a claim. It only presupposes that monitoring happens and that drift and legitimate evolution can both occur. Neither presupposition conflicts with a, which says only that monitoring, along with constraints and verification, derives from quality and is not a starting point of its own. Concrete example: a team defines quality first. It derives constraints, verification checks and monitoring from that definition, so none of the three is an independent starting point. During monitoring, it treats a change as legitimate evolution if the change follows an approved update to the quality definition, and as drift if it departs from the current definition without such an update. Every clause of a holds, and b's question has a coherent setting and answer.

Statement b is a question, so it asserts nothing that a could contradict. Its only presupposition is that quality is either a property of the result or of the task-result relation. Concrete example: quality has exactly the attributes listed in a, and quality is relational. 'Fitness for purpose' already ties the result to a task, and the other attributes (verifiability, performance, security, resilience, maintainability) can be judged against that task's requirements. Every clause of a holds, and b's question has a consistent answer. Answering 'a property of the result' would also not conflict with a, since a's list does not settle the question.

Statement b is a question, so it asserts nothing that could clash with a. At most it presupposes that measurement has dimensions and that product quality can be told apart from process quality. Concrete example: quality attributes are defined as fitness for purpose, verifiability, performance, security, resilience and maintainability (satisfying a). Measurement is described along dimensions such as accuracy, precision and timeliness. Product quality is judged by assessing the delivered artifact against those attributes, while process quality is judged by auditing the development procedures. Someone asks b, and it is answered this way. Every clause of a holds and b's presuppositions are met, so nothing conflicts.

The two statements cover different steps: (a) says what a verification outputs, and (b) lists how someone may respond to that output. Example: a verification returns the diagnosis 'clause 3 of the deliverable deviates from the agreed scope', not a yes or no. The reviewer then chooses one of the listed responses, such as 'correct', or 'accept with reservations'. The verification still returns a diagnosis rather than a verdict, and the response is one of the permitted options. 'Accept' is a response to the diagnosis, not a yes/no returned by the verification, so the two do not clash.

Statement b is a table that classifies kinds of slop: an undefined term, a task without verification, a claim of verification without evidence, and so on. It never says what a verification returns, so nothing in it requires a yes/no result. Concrete example: in a work containing this table, a verification of a spec returns 'completeness: term X used and not defined; truthfulness: claim of verification at step 3 lacks evidence' rather than 'pass/fail'. That satisfies a (a diagnosis, not a yes or a no) and is consistent with every row of b.

Example: requirements are formalised once in a decidable description logic, and the interpretive choices made during formalisation are recorded. Verification over those axioms then returns a report rather than a verdict. The report lists each minimal unsatisfiable subset, e.g. {A ⊑ B, A ⊑ ¬B, A(x)}, and each redundant axiom, e.g. C ⊑ D entailed by the rest. That satisfies a, since the output is a diagnosis, not a yes or a no. It also satisfies b: contradictions and redundancies are countable as MUSes and entailed elements, the judgement sits in formalisation, and the logic is decidable with description logics as the candidate. Decidability means the underlying satisfiability checks terminate with yes/no answers, but it does not require verification's overall output to be a bare yes/no. Moving the judgement to formalisation leaves verification computing the diagnosis, which a permits.

Example: until a logic is chosen, a verification sends each pair of term-sharing elements alone to anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 at temperature 0, using calibration/contradiction-v2/text.txt identified by its SHA-256 hash. One pair comes back 'contradiction, the requirements X and Y cannot hold together'. Another comes back 'compatible, with example E'. A third comes back 'refer' and is escalated to the user. A fourth gets a transport failure, which counts as no decision. The verification returns this per-pair report: the decisions, the named requirements, the example, the escalation and an 'incomplete' status. That report is a diagnosis, not a bare yes or no, which satisfies a. Every clause of b also holds. b's replies come in three kinds and carry reasons or examples, so they are not a yes/no answer. b's incomplete outcome can itself be reported as part of the diagnosis.

Example: a verification of document D runs a judgement that produces the diagnosis 'claim 3 is unsupported; it conflicts with section 2'. That judgement is recorded with hash(D), hash(template), models M1 and M2, N=5 and k=3. A later verification reads the record and finds all hashes unchanged, so it does not judge again and returns the stored diagnosis. If D's hash changes, it judges again and returns a new diagnosis. Every verification returns a diagnosis rather than a yes or no, which satisfies a. Every judgement is recorded with the required fields and re-judging happens only on a hash change, which satisfies b. Nothing in b requires a judgement to be a binary verdict.

Example: one diagnosis finds a deviation that is tolerable within the agreement, so the team handles it at its own level by correcting it (or by accepting it, with or without reservations). Another diagnosis finds a deviation that is not tolerable, so it is escalated, and the higher level then reviews the agreement or the intent. Every response used comes from a's list. Everything tolerable is resolved locally and everything intolerable is escalated, as b requires. Statement a's list does not forbid b's tolerability rule for choosing between local resolution and escalation, and b does not exclude any response in a.

The two statements cover different things and do not conflict. Statement a lists the possible responses to a diagnosis: accept, accept with reservations, correct, escalate, or review the agreement or the intent. Statement b is a table of seven figures (form, fit, economy, completeness, order, sharpness, truthfulness), each paired with an image and with the kinds of slop it covers in this work. Neither constrains the other. Concrete example: one review framework uses b's table to diagnose problems and a's list to respond. A reviewer flags an 'economy' problem because the same thing is said twice, and the response is 'correct'. Another flags a 'fit' problem because an element is not traceable to the intent, and the response is 'review the agreement or the intent'. Another flags a 'truthfulness' problem because a claim of verification lacks evidence, and the response is 'escalate'. Every row of b stays as stated, and every response comes from a's list, so both statements hold together.

The two statements cover different things. Statement a lists the allowed responses to a diagnosis. Statement b describes how the comparison loop is run. Example satisfying both: in a workflow, any diagnosis can receive exactly one of these responses: accept, accept with reservations, correct, escalate, or review the agreement or the intent. Separately, the comparison loop is handed off as a delegated task under its own agreement. It runs with no user intervention inside the loop, and the user validates its result at the end. The user's final validation is a check on the loop's output, not a response to a diagnosis, so it does not break a's closed list. Nothing in either statement restricts the other.

Example: a comparison loop runs as a delegated task under its own agreement. While comparing, it finds only discrepancies within the agreed tolerance and resolves them itself, without asking the user. That satisfies b's 'autonomous inside' and a's rule that tolerable matters are resolved at their own level. Had a discrepancy exceeded the tolerance, the loop would escalate it. a requires that, and b does not forbid it; a simply marks where the loop's autonomy ends. When the loop finishes, the user validates the result, satisfying b's end validation. Every clause of both statements holds.

b is phrased as a question, so taken literally it asserts nothing that could clash with a. Even if b is read as the claim 'autonomy depends on verifiability, and more verifiable results can be delegated more', both can hold together. Example: under a service agreement, a team's output counts as 'tolerable' when it can be checked against agreed acceptance tests and falls within agreed limits. The team settles such issues itself. Anything outside those limits, or anything that cannot be verified, is escalated. Here tolerability marks the boundary of autonomy, as a requires. Tolerability is itself determined by verifiability, so autonomy depends on verifiability and the more verifiable a result is, the more it is delegated, as b requires. Neither statement says its criterion is the only one.

Both can hold in one framework, for example a writing-style guide. A says impeccable work is beautiful, slop introduces ugliness, and gives two images: a line that breaks the metre and a forced puzzle piece. B's table reuses those same two images, under 'form' and 'fit'. It then adds five more figures and maps each to concrete kinds of slop, such as a term with two meanings or the same thing said twice. Take a document containing a term with two meanings. That term is slop, it introduces ugliness (A), and it is pictured as the line that breaks the metre (A and B). B only adds detail. It never denies that impeccable work is beautiful, and A never limits slop or its images to the two A names.

The two statements fit together. b classifies text: headings are unmeasured labels, and any other text is slop of form. a says slop introduces ugliness and impeccable things are beautiful. Example: artefact X has a heading 'Summary' and one element, with nothing extra, so it is impeccable and beautiful. Artefact Y has a heading, an element and a stray sentence outside them. That sentence is slop of form and makes Y ugly, like a line that breaks a poem's metre or a forced puzzle piece. Every clause of both statements holds. b's 'any other text' is ambiguous: it may mean text outside headings and elements, or all non-heading text. This does not change the result. On the broader reading, elements count as slop and make artefacts ugly, and a never says artefacts must be beautiful.

The two statements fit together. Example: a poem in which no line breaks the metre and no element breaks any other figure has a violation sum of zero. By b it is impeccable, and a lets it be beautiful. A second poem with exactly one line that breaks the metre has slop 1 (an unweighted count of one violation), so it is not impeccable, and that slop introduces ugliness, as a says. The forced puzzle piece also fits b's rule that an element counts in every figure it breaks. Statement b only says how slop is counted, and statement a only says how slop and impeccability relate to beauty and ugliness. Neither forbids what the other requires, whether 'something impeccable' is read as 'some' or as 'every' impeccable thing.

The two statements cover different topics and can both be true. Example: impeccable work is beautiful, and slop adds ugliness, like a line that breaks a poem's metre or a puzzle piece forced into the wrong place. Separately, a statistical verifier is tested against a corpus with known slop, just as candidates are. Evaluating a verifier on sloppy test material does not require anything impeccable to be ugly or slop to be beautiful, and the aesthetic claims put no limits on how a verifier is evaluated.

Statement b's table lists exactly the seven figures named in a (form, fit, economy, completeness, order, sharpness, truthfulness), none missing and none added. Its image and slop columns are extra detail. Concrete example: one work defines those seven figures and gives each the image and slop description shown in b's table. That satisfies a's list and every row of b.

The two statements cover different matters. Statement a lists seven figures, and b describes what an artefact is made of and how stray text is classed. Example: a review scheme whose figures are exactly form, fit, economy, completeness, order, sharpness and truthfulness. Under it, an artefact holds the heading 'Summary' plus one element. The heading is treated as a label and not measured, and any text outside headings and elements would count as slop of form. 'Slop of form' fits naturally with 'form' being one of the figures. Even if 'any other text' meant everything except headings, which would make elements slop of form, nothing in a forbids that, so both readings give the same answer.

Statement a names seven figures: form, fit, economy, completeness, order, sharpness and truthfulness. Statement b's table lists exactly those seven figures, in the same order, with no additions or omissions, and gives each a violation definition. Example satisfying both: a checking scheme whose only figures are these seven, each counting violations as b defines them (e.g. form counts malformed headers, duplicate identifiers, etc.; truthfulness counts claims without evidence). The violation definitions are extra detail that a neither states nor rules out, so every clause of both statements holds.

Statement a names seven figures. Statement b sets an unweighted counting rule over whatever the figures are, so b can use a's list directly. Example: the seven figures are form, fit, economy, completeness, order, sharpness and truthfulness. In artefact A, one element breaks form and order, so it counts once in each, and no other violations occur. A's slop is 1+1 = 2, so A is not impeccable. Artefact B breaks no figure, so its slop is 0 and B is impeccable. Every clause of both statements holds.

A names seven figures: form, fit, economy, completeness, order, sharpness and truthfulness. B defines error as the symmetric difference between detected and true violations, each keyed by figure, element and detail. B also sets the pass rule: zero error on every corpus and identical output on two runs. Example satisfying both: the figures are exactly A's seven. On corpus 1 the true violations are {(form, element E1, detail D1), (order, E2, D2)}, and a candidate detects exactly that set, so the error is 0. On corpus 2 the true set is empty and the candidate detects nothing, so the error is 0. The candidate produces the same output on both runs, so it passes. Nothing in A limits how violations are counted or how passing is judged, and nothing in B limits which figures exist.

Example: an artefact made only of headings (labels, not measured) and elements, with no other text. B's rule that any other text is slop of form then applies to nothing. A's table still sets what counts as slop in this work: in form, a term with two meanings or an element in the wrong language; in fit, contradicting or untraceable elements; in economy, repetition; in completeness, an undefined term or a task without verification; in order, a term used before its definition; in sharpness, a two-reading sentence; in truthfulness, a verification claim without evidence. A never says headings are measured or that non-element text is acceptable. B adds one more case of form slop, which is extra detail, not a conflict. Even if A's form list were read as exhaustive, this example contains no text of B's extra kind, so every clause of both statements holds.

Statement a is a taxonomy of what counts as slop: elements in the wrong language, contradictions, repetition, undefined terms, ambiguous sentences and unsupported verification claims. Statement b gives the syntax of an element. Neither requires anything the other forbids. Concrete example: a specification that includes a's table as its quality criteria. Its elements are written as '[R1] {type: requirement; verify: unit test}' followed by one unambiguous, non-repeated sentence, which runs until the next header line '[R2] {...}' or a heading. Every term in it is defined before use, nothing contradicts anything else, and no verification is claimed without evidence. That document satisfies b's format and avoids every slop category in a.

The two statements cover different things, so one work can satisfy both. Statement a lists seven quality figures (form, fit, economy, completeness, order, sharpness, truthfulness) and the slop each one names. Statement b sets the metadata keys an element carries. Nothing in a forbids or requires anything that b controls, and nothing in b conflicts with a. Example work: it adopts table a as its quality taxonomy and contains three elements tagged per b. E1: kind=definition, defines='slop', variants=['defect'], status=proposal. E2: kind=rule, derives=[INTENT], status=proposal. E3: kind=claim, derives=[E1, E2], evidence='test log 3', status=proposal. These satisfy every clause of b. Only E1 has defines and variants. E2 and E3, the non-definitions, have derives. Only E3 has evidence. All carry status=proposal because none has been validated. They also avoid a's listed slop. 'Slop' is defined in E1 before E3 uses it. E3's claim has evidence. Each element traces to the intent or to other elements. Nothing is repeated, and nothing is ambiguous or in the wrong language. The two statements even align: a counts a claim of verification without evidence as slop, and b gives claims an evidence key.

Statement a is a table classifying kinds of slop: two meanings, wrong language, contradiction, untraceable element, repetition, undefined term, unverified task, term before definition, two readings, unevidenced verification claim. Statement b is a marking convention: every use of a term goes in double square brackets, in a variant its definition declares, and unmarked text is ordinary vocabulary. Neither forbids what the other requires. Concrete example: a work states the convention in b and includes the table in a. Its table words ('term', 'slop', 'figure') are unmarked, so under b they are ordinary vocabulary and need no definition. Wherever the work uses a defined term, it writes it as [[term-variant]] after that term's definition. Every clause of both statements then holds together.

Concrete example: the work's glossary first defines, in order, 'term', 'definition', 'element', 'intent', 'verification', 'evidence', 'slop' and 'figure', each entry using only words defined above it and never its own word. The glossary then contains this table as its final entries, one per figure (form, fit, economy, completeness, order, sharpness, truthfulness). No row repeats its own figure name, and every glossary term a row relies on is defined earlier. No definition appears anywhere outside the glossary. This satisfies b under either reading of a. If the table merely classifies kinds of slop rather than defining anything, it can sit anywhere. If its rows count as definitions, the arrangement above keeps them inside the glossary and properly ordered. The table's own norms, such as 'a term used before its definition' counting as slop, agree with b.

Whether the two tables conflict depends on whether each one sorts defects into exclusive figures, or exhaustively lists what counts under each figure.

Reading 1: the tables are non-exclusive, and B is an operational check refining A's informal images. They are then compatible. A term given two definitions would count as A-form slop ('a term with two meanings') and as a B-sharpness violation ('each term with more than one definition'). Several other rows also line up:
- A's wrong-language element matches B's Spanish-stopword check.
- A's contradicting element matches B's minimal unsatisfiable subsets.
- A's 'same thing said twice' matches B's redundancy measure.
- A's undefined term matches B's undeclared marked term.
- A's term used before its definition matches B's order row.
- A's unevidenced verification claim matches B's 'claim without evidence'.

Reading 2: each defect belongs to exactly one figure, and B's list is exhaustive. Then there is a conflict:
- A files a term with two meanings under form, while B files a multiply-defined term under sharpness.
- A's completeness includes 'a task without verification', which B's completeness row (only undeclared marked terms) does not cover.

The pair does not say whether the figures partition the defects or whether B's list is complete. The two readings give opposite answers.

Statement a lists seven figures and the kinds of slop that violate each. Statement b adds a counting rule over those figures: an element counts once in every figure it breaks, slop is the unweighted sum, and an artefact is impeccable exactly when that sum is zero. Nothing in a sets weights or limits an element to one figure, so b only adds detail. Example satisfying both: an artefact contains one term with two meanings that also makes its sentence have two readings. That element breaks form and sharpness. It also contains a task without verification, which breaks completeness, and nothing else. Its slop is 1+1+1 = 3, so it is not impeccable. A second artefact with no violation in any of the seven figures has slop 0 and is impeccable. Both cases follow a's table and b's rule.

Both can hold in one example. Statement a is a table mapping quality figures to images and kinds of slop. Two of those kinds are 'an element that contradicts another' (fit) and 'the same thing said twice' (economy). Statement b says contradiction and redundancy become countable once elements are written as logical formulas, using a decidable logic such as a description logic: a contradiction is a minimal unsatisfiable subset, and an element is redundant when the rest entails it. Concrete example: a specification is audited against a's table, and its elements are also encoded as axioms in a description logic such as ALC. Two axioms that are jointly unsatisfiable form a minimal unsatisfiable subset, which counts as 'fit' slop. An axiom entailed by the others counts as 'economy' slop. These judgements are made once, at formalisation, and recorded. Every row of a's table still applies. b's entailment-based redundancy is broader than literal repetition, but b does not claim to redefine a's category. b's shift 'from verification to formalisation' concerns how the judgement is made; it does not affect a's separate rule that a task without verification is slop. Neither statement forbids anything the other requires.

Example: a work's style guide contains table a, which lists 'the same thing said twice' as economy slop. Its review procedure follows b. Until a logic is chosen, redundancy is judged by a versioned yes-or-no question with typed yes and no criteria. The question goes through the OpenRouter Decisions API to the three pinned models. Say typesafe/jev-1.14 repeats its output exactly, so it runs once; the other two run three times each. Only elements that share a term are compared. Statement a says what counts as slop; statement b says how redundancy is judged in the interim. No clause of b denies that repetition is slop. A restates the same point twice, but the restatements share no term, would be slop under a yet go unchecked under b. That is a gap in detection, not a contradiction, because a does not require that every instance be caught.

Example: one specification document contains a's table as its taxonomy of slop, so 'an element that contradicts another' is slop under fit, 'a task without verification' is slop under completeness, and so on. Its verification section states b's procedure. Until a logic is chosen, contradiction is judged by anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 at temperature 0, using calibration/contradiction-v2/text.txt identified by its SHA-256 hash. Each pair of elements sharing a term is sent alone. Replies are contradiction (naming the clashing requirements), compatible (with a satisfying example), or refer. A refer goes to the user. A schema or transport failure leaves verification incomplete and is not a decision. Both hold together: a classifies what counts as slop, and b says how one category, contradiction, is detected. A verification left incomplete under b would count as slop under a, but that is a classification, not a conflict between the statements.

Example: a project uses table (a) as its taxonomy of slop, mapping figures such as 'completeness' to 'a term used and not defined; a task without verification'. Its verifier follows (b). Each judgement is stored with the input hash, the template hash, the models, N and k. A later verification reads this record and judges again only if the input hash or the template hash differs. Statement (a) defines categories of defects. Statement (b) describes how verification results are recorded and reused. Nothing in (a) forbids caching judgements, and (b) does not change the taxonomy, so every clause of both holds at once. Under (a)'s own criteria, (b) is also not 'a claim of verification without evidence', because each judgement keeps its hashes and parameters.

Statement a is a taxonomy of slop types grouped by figure, for example 'the same thing said twice' under economy. Statement b says the statistical verifier is scored against a corpus with known slop, just as any candidate is. Both can hold at once. Example: a project defines slop with exactly this seven-row table. It builds a corpus seeded with labelled instances of those types, such as a term used before its definition, a sentence with two readings, and a claim of verification without evidence. It then measures the statistical verifier on that corpus, as it measures other candidates. Nothing in a forbids evaluating the verifier, and b adds no slop category that conflicts with the table. Evaluating the verifier also does not create a 'task without verification' or an unevidenced verification claim.

Statement a is a table of seven figures (form, fit, economy, completeness, order, sharpness, truthfulness), each with the kinds of slop it covers. Statement b defines how a candidate detector is scored: error is the symmetric difference between detected and true violation sets, with each violation identified by figure, element and detail. A candidate passes only with zero error on every corpus and identical output on two runs. The two fit together: a supplies the figures that b's violations are labelled with. Concrete example: one corpus has a single document in which the term 'node' has two meanings. Its true set is {(form, 'node', term with two meanings)}. The candidate reports exactly that triple on both runs, so the symmetric difference is 0 on the only corpus and the outputs are identical. The candidate passes, every clause of b holds, and every violation uses a figure and slop type from a's table.

Statement a is a table that classifies kinds of slop, such as 'a task without verification' or 'a term used and not defined'. Statement b describes the comparison loop as a delegated task with its own agreement, autonomous inside and validated by the user at the end. Concrete example: a working document contains the table from a and a comparison loop defined as in b. The loop runs on its own and the user validates its result when it finishes. That end validation is the task's verification, so the loop is not 'a task without verification'. Nothing in b is said twice, contradicts the table, or claims verification without evidence. Both statements hold together.

Statement a is a table that maps quality figures (form, fit, economy, completeness, order, sharpness, truthfulness) to images and to kinds of slop. Statement b is only a question. It asserts nothing, so it adds no requirement that could conflict with a. Concrete example: a writing guide contains a's table exactly as given, with each figure, image and slop description, and then asks a reader, 'Is quality a property of the result, or of the relation between task and result?' Both hold. Answering b either way would still fit the table. Some entries look like properties of the result alone, such as 'the same thing said twice'. Others are relational, such as 'an element not traceable to the intent' and 'a task without verification'.

Example artefact: a heading line '## Findings', then the header line '[E1] {type=claim; status=draft}', then the text 'Rates rose in Q3.', then the heading '## Notes'. The artefact consists only of headings and one element, so a holds with no stray text. The element starts with its identifier in square brackets followed by key-value metadata in braces separated by a semicolon, and its text runs until the next heading, so b holds. Even if a's 'any other text' is read as all non-heading text, including element text, being slop of form, b neither forbids that label nor conflicts with it, so the same example still satisfies both.

Statement b lists metadata keys but never says they sit outside elements, so the metadata can be read as part of each element. Example: an artefact with the heading 'Definitions' (a label, not measured) and one element carrying 'kind: definition', 'defines: term X', 'variants: X-alt' and 'status: proposal'. It has no derives key, which is allowed in a definition, and no evidence key, which is reserved for claims. A second element could have 'kind: rule', 'derives: INTENT' and 'status: proposal'. The artefact contains only headings and elements, so no text counts as slop of form, and every key condition in b is met.

Both statements can hold together. Example: an artefact with one heading 'Goals' and one well-formed element E1 of a valid kind, with all required keys and a unique identifier. E1 derives from INTENT, uses no vague words, has supporting evidence, and there is no text outside headings and elements. a's rule that any non-heading, non-element text is slop of form matches b's form violation 'text outside elements and headings'. a's rule that headings are not measured holds because none of b's figures counts headings. b's 'malformed header' most naturally means an element's header line, which sits alongside identifier, kind and required key, rather than a heading. If 'header' were read as a heading, a's rule would be in tension with b, but the natural reading is consistent.

Example: an artefact made of one heading and one element, with no other text, where the element breaks no figure. Statement a holds: the artefact consists only of headings and elements, the heading is unmeasured, and there is no other text that would be slop of form. Statement b holds: the element breaks no figure, so it counts nowhere, the unweighted sum of violations is zero, and the artefact is impeccable. If other text did appear, a calls it slop of form; this fits b provided form is one of the figures whose violations are summed. Neither statement rules that out.

The two statements address different things. Statement a defines what an artefact is made of: headings and elements, with any other text counted as slop. Statement b defines how elements are formalised so that contradictions and redundancy can be counted. Example satisfying both: an artefact contains the heading 'Staff rules', which is an unmeasured label, and three elements: 'Every manager is an employee', 'Bob is a manager' and 'Bob is an employee'. It contains no other text, so it has no slop of form. Each element is formalised once in the decidable description logic ALC as Manager ⊑ Employee, Manager(bob) and Employee(bob). That mapping is recorded in a separate formalisation record outside the artefact. The set is satisfiable, so it contains no minimal unsatisfiable subset and the contradiction count is 0. Employee(bob) is entailed by the other two formulas, so it is redundant and the redundancy count is 1. Verification then works from the recorded formulas. Every clause of a and b holds. Statement b never requires the artefact to contain text beyond its headings and elements.

Example: an artefact contains only the heading 'Pets' and two elements, 'Cats purr.' and 'Cats meow.'. It has no other text, so nothing is slop of form. The heading is a label and is not measured. No logic has been chosen yet, so redundancy is judged by a statistical verifier. Version 1 of a yes-or-no question, with typed criteria for yes and for no, is sent through the OpenRouter Decisions API to the three pinned models. microsoft/microsoft-decision-1.1 repeats its output exactly, so it runs once. pplx-decider-v1.2 and jev-1.14 do not, so each runs three times. Only the two elements are compared, because they share the term 'cats'. Statement a governs what an artefact contains, and the verifier's question is not part of the artefact. Every clause of both statements holds.

The two statements cover different matters. Statement a defines what an artefact is made of: headings and elements. Headings are unmeasured labels, and any other text counts as slop of form. Statement b sets out how contradiction between elements is judged until a logic is chosen. A concrete example satisfies both. Take an artefact with one heading, 'Rules', and two elements that share the term 'refund': 'Refunds are issued within 30 days' and 'Refunds require a receipt'. The heading is not measured, and there is no other text. That pair alone is sent to anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 at temperature 0, using calibration/contradiction-v2/text.txt identified by its SHA-256 hash. The model replies 'compatible' with the example of a receipted refund issued on day 10. Had it replied 'refer', the case would go to the user. A reply that failed the schema, or a transport failure, would leave verification incomplete and would not count as a decision. None of b's clauses about elements, pairs, replies or failures conflicts with a's definition of headings, elements or slop.

The statements cover different things. Statement a sets out how an artefact is built and scored: it is made of headings and elements, headings are unmeasured labels, and any other text counts as slop of form. Statement b says the statistical verifier, like any candidate, is tested on a corpus with known slop. Example satisfying both: artefacts contain only headings and elements, headings are not measured, and any stray text is labelled slop of form. The verifier is then run on a reference corpus where slop is known, including artefacts with such stray text, and is scored the same way other candidates are. Neither statement forbids or requires anything the other rules out.

The two statements cover different matters and impose no conflicting requirements. Statement a defines what an artefact contains and how its text is classified. Statement b defines how a candidate's error is scored and when the candidate passes. Concrete example: an artefact has the heading 'Results', which is an unmeasured label, and one element, 'Figure 1 caption', with no other text, so there is no slop of form. A candidate checks each corpus. On every corpus, its detected set of violations, each identified by figure, element and detail (e.g., {(Figure 1, caption, missing units)}), exactly equals the true set. The symmetric difference is therefore empty and the error is 0. Two runs produce identical output, so the candidate passes. Every clause of both statements holds.

The two statements cover different things: (a) sets the header syntax and where an element's text ends, and (b) lists the allowed metadata keys and their constraints. One element satisfies both: the header line `[R1] {kind: rule; derives: INTENT; status: proposal}`, followed by its rule text and ending at the next header line. It has the identifier in square brackets, then key-value pairs in braces separated by semicolons, as (a) requires. For (b), kind is rule, so derives is present as required outside a definition and holds `INTENT`. It omits defines, variants and evidence, which are restricted to definitions or claims. Status is proposal, consistent with not yet being validated. Nothing in either statement conflicts.

Statement a defines the element format: a bracketed identifier, then braced semicolon-separated key-value metadata, then text running to the next header or heading. Statement b only classifies violations, one of which is a malformed header. That presupposes a header format like a's and does not conflict with it. Concrete example: a single element with header '[I1] {kind=INTENT; owner=Ann}' followed by the text 'Ship the report Friday.' This satisfies a. Under b it shows no violations: the header is well formed, the identifier is unique, the kind is plausibly valid, no text sits outside elements, there are no Spanish stopwords, the element is itself INTENT and so traceable, there are no marked terms or definitions, and there are no vague words or unsupported claims. Both statements hold together.

The two statements cover different things. Statement a sets the element syntax, and statement b sets how violations are counted. One example satisfies both. Take an artefact with two elements. The first starts with the header line `[E1] {kind: note; owner: Ana}`, and its text 'First body.' runs until the header line `[E2] {kind: note; owner: Ben}`. E2's text 'Second body.' runs until the heading '## End'. Now suppose there are two figures, F1 and F2. E1 breaks both, so it counts once in each. E2 breaks neither. That gives 2 violations in total, summed with no weights, so the slop is 2 and the artefact is not impeccable. If no element broke any figure, the sum would be 0 and the artefact would be impeccable. Nothing in either statement conflicts with the other.

Statement a fixes the textual layout of an element: a bracketed identifier, brace-delimited semicolon-separated metadata, and text running to the next header or heading. Statement b is about writing element content as formulas in a decidable logic so that contradiction (a minimal unsatisfiable subset) and redundancy (the rest entails the element) can be counted. Neither constrains what the other governs. Example: a document has element '[E1] {author=ann; status=draft}' with text 'Cat ⊑ Animal', element '[E2] {author=bob; status=final}' with text 'Cat ⊑ ¬Animal', and element '[E3] {author=ann; status=final}' with text 'Cat ⊑ Animal'. Each element runs to the next header line. The text is in the description logic ALC, which is decidable, and the judgement is formalised once and recorded. Ignoring E3, {E1, E2} is the minimal unsatisfiable subset, so it counts as a contradiction. E3 is redundant because E1 entails it. Every clause of both statements holds.

The two statements cover different things: (a) sets the element syntax, and (b) sets how redundancy is judged before a logic is chosen. Neither limits the other. Example: a document has element '[E1] {type: claim; version: 2}' followed by text that runs to the next header '[E2] {type: claim; version: 1}', whose text runs to the next heading. No logic has been chosen. Redundancy between E1 and E2, which share the term 'cache', is judged by verifier question v1.0. It is a yes-or-no question with typed yes and no criteria, sent through the OpenRouter Decisions API to the pinned panel microsoft/microsoft-decision-1.1, perplexity/pplx-decider-v1.2 and typesafe/jev-1.14. The microsoft model's output repeats exactly, so it is run once; the other two are run three times each. Elements with no shared term are not compared. Every clause of both statements holds.

The two statements cover different things. Statement a defines how an element is written. Statement b defines how contradictions between elements are judged before a logic is chosen. A single system can satisfy both. Example: element E1 is written as '[E1] {term: retention; owner: ops}' and its text runs until the next header line. Element E2 is written as '[E2] {term: retention; owner: legal}' with its own text. Both share the term 'retention', so the pair (E1, E2) is sent alone to anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 at temperature 0. The prompt uses calibration/contradiction-v2/text.txt, identified by its SHA-256 hash. The model replies 'refer', so the pair is escalated to the user. In a separate run, a malformed reply or a network error marks the verification incomplete and records no decision. Every clause of a (bracketed identifier, braced semicolon-separated key-value metadata, text ending at the next header or heading) and every clause of b (model, temperature, hashed template, one pair per request, three reply types, refer escalation, failures not counting as decisions) holds at the same time.

The two statements cover different things. (a) defines the syntax of an element; (b) defines how a candidate's error is scored and when it may pass. One scenario satisfies both. A corpus contains the header line '[E1] {type=claim; figure=2}', followed by text that runs until the next header '[E2] {...}' or a heading, as (a) requires. A candidate checks each corpus for violations, each identified by (figure, element, detail), e.g. (2, E1, missing key 'source'). On every corpus its detected set equals the true set, so the symmetric difference is empty and the error is 0. Two runs produce identical output. The candidate therefore meets (b)'s necessary conditions for passing, and nothing in either statement conflicts.

Statement a defines the metadata keys and statement b lists violation categories; nothing in one rules out the other. Example: a scheme uses exactly a's keys and b's checks. Element D1 has kind: definition, defines: 'cliente', variants: 'clientes', status: proposal, and no derives key. Element R1 has kind: rule, derives: INTENT, status: proposal, and uses the marked term 'cliente' after D1. Element C1 has kind: claim, derives: R1, evidence: an audit reference, status: proposal. On form, R1 and C1 carry the required derives key and D1 is exempt, matching a. On fit, R1 reaches INTENT, C1 reaches it through R1, and D1 is traceable because its term is used by R1, which fits definitions having no derives. Truthfulness is satisfied because C1 carries evidence, the key a allows only in claims. Order, completeness and sharpness are also satisfied: one definition per term, defined before use, and no vague words. b's treatment of a claim without evidence as a violation adds detail and does not conflict with a.

The two statements cover different things. Statement a sets the metadata schema for elements. Statement b sets how violations are counted. Neither constrains the other. Example: an artefact holds one element with kind: definition, defines: X, variants: [X'] and status: proposal. It has no derives and no evidence, which a allows for a definition. Under b, that element breaks no figure, so its count is zero in every figure. The unweighted sum over all figures is 0, so slop is 0 and the artefact is impeccable. Adding a claim element with kind: claim, derives: [INTENT], evidence: E and status: proposal also satisfies a. If that claim broke two figures, it would count once in each, and the slop of 2 would follow b's rule. This shows both statements can hold together.

The two statements cover different things. Statement a sets out the metadata schema for each element. Statement b proposes writing the elements as formulas in a decidable logic, so that contradictions and redundancies can be counted. Nothing in a forbids a formal body for an element, and b needs no extra metadata key. Concrete example: Element E1 has kind: definition, defines: Customer, variants: [client], status: proposal, and no derives. Its body is the description-logic axiom Customer ⊑ ∃hasAccount.Account. Element E2 has kind: rule, derives: [E1, INTENT], status: proposal. Its body is Customer ⊑ ≤1 hasAccount. Element E3 has kind: claim, derives: [AGREEMENT], evidence: interview notes, status: proposal. Its body is a Customer individual with two distinct accounts. During formalisation, a decidable description-logic reasoner finds that {E2, E3} is a minimal unsatisfiable subset, which is one contradiction. It also checks each element for entailment by the rest and finds none redundant. These results are recorded once. Every clause of a holds: each kind is one of the four allowed, defines and variants appear only in the definition, derives appears on the non-definitions with allowed values, evidence appears only in the claim, and status is proposal. Every clause of b holds as well.

The two statements cover different things: (a) defines the metadata schema for elements, and (b) defines how redundancy is judged before a logic is chosen. Concrete example: no logic has been chosen yet. Element R1 has kind: rule, derives: [INTENT], status: proposal. It has no defines, variants or evidence, which is allowed for a rule. Element D1 has kind: definition, defines: [term T], variants: [T'], status: proposal, and no derives, since derives is required only outside definitions. Element C1 has kind: claim, derives: [D1], evidence: [...], status: proposal. R1 and C1 both use term T, so they are compared. D1 and an unrelated question Q1 share no term and are not compared. Redundancy is judged by versioned question v1, 'Is C1 redundant given R1?', with typed criteria for yes and for no. It is sent through the OpenRouter Decisions API to the pinned panel of microsoft/microsoft-decision-1.1, perplexity/pplx-decider-v1.2 and typesafe/jev-1.14. Suppose microsoft's output repeats exactly: it is run once, and the other two are each run three times. Every clause of both statements holds.

The two statements cover different matters. (a) sets the metadata keys for elements. (b) sets the procedure for judging contradiction between pairs of elements. No requirement in one limits the other. Concrete example: element E1 is a definition with kind=definition, defines=['term'], variants=['terms'] and status=proposal, with no derives and no evidence. Element E2 is a claim with kind=claim, derives=['E1'], evidence=['source'] and status=proposal. No logic has been chosen yet, so the pair (E1, E2), which shares 'term', is sent alone to anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 at temperature 0. The prompt uses the template calibration/contradiction-v2/text.txt, identified by its SHA-256 hash. The reply is 'compatible' with an example satisfying both elements. If the reply had been refer, it would go to the user. A schema failure or transport failure would leave verification incomplete, with no decision. This satisfies every clause of both statements.

The two statements cover different things. Statement a sets out the metadata schema for elements. Statement b defines how a checker candidate is scored and when it passes. Nothing in one limits the other. Concrete example: an element has kind: rule, derives: [INTENT] and status: proposal. It has no defines, variants or evidence keys, which is allowed because it is not a definition or a claim. A definition element carries defines and variants, has no derives, and has status: proposal. A candidate is tested on a single corpus whose true violations are {(figure 1, element R2, 'derives missing')}. It detects exactly that set, so the symmetric difference is 0 and the error is 0. Two runs give identical output, so the candidate passes. Every clause of both statements holds at the same time.

Example: a glossary is the only place definitions appear. Definition 1 declares the term 'node' with variants 'node' and 'nodes' and is written entirely in ordinary, unmarked vocabulary: 'a point in the network'. Definition 2 declares 'edge' as 'a link between two [[nodes]]', using only the earlier term, in a declared variant. Elsewhere, every use of a term is bracketed, e.g. 'each [[edge]] joins [[nodes]]', and unbracketed words are ordinary vocabulary. No definition uses a later term or its own term. This assumes the entry that names and declares a term is not itself a 'use' of that term, which is the natural reading of 'never its own term' as forbidding circular definitions.

Statement a sets the marking rule: every use of a term is written as [[variant]], and unmarked text counts as ordinary vocabulary. Statement b lists what counts as a violation, including 'an unmarked occurrence of a declared variant' and 'each distinct marked term that no definition declares'. These two enforce a's rule rather than conflict with it. Calling unmarked text ordinary vocabulary does not grant permission to leave a declared variant unmarked, so b can treat that as a form violation without contradicting a.
