Concrete example: an artefact defines the term 'budget' with variants 'budget' and 'budgets'. Its only element reads 'The [[budget]] is fixed.' That element is traceable to INTENT and is placed after the definition. Every term use is marked with a declared variant, and no declared variant appears unmarked. Both a and b hold, and b's table reports no form or completeness violation.

Example: in a spec, the term [[ledger]] is defined with variants [[ledger]] and [[ledgers]]. Every use of the term is written in one of those bracketed variants, and the bracketing is the formalisation. Unbracketed words are ordinary vocabulary. No logic has been chosen yet, so redundancy is judged by a versioned yes/no decision question with typed yes and no criteria. It is sent through the OpenRouter Decisions API to the three pinned models. microsoft/microsoft-decision-1.1 repeats its output exactly, so it runs once; the other two run three times each. Two requirements, R1 and R2, both contain [[ledger]], so they share a term and are compared. A requirement with no shared marked term is not compared. Statement a sets a marking convention and b sets a comparison procedure that relies on marked terms, so all clauses hold together. Even if b's own text were governed by a, its unbracketed words would simply count as ordinary vocabulary, which a permits.

The two statements govern different things. a sets a notation rule: each use of a defined term is written in double square brackets, using one of the variants its definition declares, and unmarked text is ordinary vocabulary. b sets a verification procedure for judging contradiction before a logic is chosen. Concrete example: a specification defines a term 'Order' with variants 'Order' and 'Orders'. Two elements each contain '[[Order]]', and nothing unmarked is treated as a term. Because these elements share a term, the pair is sent alone to anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 at temperature 0, using calibration/contradiction-v2/text.txt identified by its SHA-256 hash. The model replies 'refer', which is escalated to the user. A schema-failing reply or a transport failure would leave verification incomplete and not count as a decision. Every clause of both statements holds. b's own unbracketed words, such as 'contradiction', are ordinary vocabulary under a, since this pair contains no definitions that make them terms.

Statement b is a taxonomy of violation types, not a claim that any violation occurs. Two of its entries match a's rules exactly: 'a definition that uses its own term' (form) and 'an element using a term before its definition' (order). b sets no rule about where definitions may live, so a's glossary-only rule adds detail without conflict. Concrete example: adopt b's table as the scoring scheme for an artefact whose only definitions sit in its glossary. The first entry, 'unit: a measured quantity', relies on no defined terms. The second, 'cell: a grouping of unit values', uses only the earlier term 'unit' and not its own term. Every clause of a holds, b's taxonomy applies unchanged, and the artefact incurs no form or order violations.

Example: a document's glossary defines, in order, 'term', 'element', 'redundancy', 'decision question', 'decision model' and then 'statistical verifier'. Each entry uses only earlier terms and never its own. No definitions appear anywhere else. Before any logic is chosen, redundancy is judged by asking a versioned yes-or-no question, v1 'Are these two elements redundant?', with typed criteria for yes and for no. The question is sent through the OpenRouter Decisions API to the pinned models microsoft/microsoft-decision-1.1, perplexity/pplx-decider-v1.2 and typesafe/jev-1.14. Suppose only microsoft/microsoft-decision-1.1 repeats its output exactly: it runs once and the other two run three times each. Only elements that share a term are compared. Statement a constrains where and how definitions are written. Statement b describes a redundancy-checking procedure. Even if b's description of 'statistical verifier' counts as a definition, it can sit in the glossary after the terms it uses, so every clause of both holds.

Example: the glossary holds all definitions in order. 'Element: a numbered statement of the specification.' 'Term: a word given a meaning in this glossary.' 'Verification: checking every pair of elements that share a term.' Each entry uses only earlier terms and never its own. Statement b sits outside the glossary as a procedural rule, not a definition. Until a logic is chosen, each pair of elements sharing a term is sent alone to anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 at temperature 0, using the template calibration/contradiction-v2/text.txt identified by its SHA-256 hash. Each reply is contradiction (naming the conflicting requirements), compatible (with a satisfying example), or refer. Refers go to the user. Schema or transport failures leave verification incomplete and count as no decision. Nothing in b requires a definition outside the glossary or a circular definition, so every clause of both statements holds.

Statement a lists what counts as a violation in each figure. Statement b adds the scoring rule: an element counts once in every figure it breaks, the slop is the unweighted sum of violation counts across figures, and an artefact is impeccable exactly when that sum is zero. Nothing in a requires weights, limits an element to one figure, or blocks summing. Economy's violation count is itself a number (size of Σ' minus its smallest equivalent subset), so it adds into the sum directly. Example: an artefact with one element that is not traceable to INTENT or AGREEMENT and contains one vague-list word. It counts once under fit and once under sharpness. With no other violations and economy at 0, the slop is 2 and the artefact is not impeccable. If those two problems are fixed, every figure is 0, the slop is 0, and the artefact is impeccable. Both statements hold in each case.

The two statements fit together. B says elements are written as decidable logical formulas, with description logics as the candidate. It defines a contradiction as a minimal unsatisfiable subset (MUS) and calls an element redundant when the rest entails it. A's table counts each MUS under 'fit' and measures economy as |Σ'| minus its smallest equivalent subset, with MUS elements excluded from Σ'. Both definitions can apply to the same system. Concrete example: an ALC artefact with e1: A ⊑ B, e2: B ⊑ C, e3: A ⊑ C, e4: A(x), e5: ¬A(x), each derived from INTENT. Assume all headers, keys and identifiers are well-formed, every element sits inside its heading, and there are no Spanish stopwords, vague words or variants. Assume every marked term (A, B, C) has exactly one definition, each placed before its first use, and every claim has evidence. Then {e4, e5} is the only MUS, so fit counts 1 and B's contradiction count is also 1. Σ' = {e1, e2, e3}, and its smallest equivalent subset is {e1, e2}, so economy is 1. B's test gives the same result: e3 is entailed by e1 and e2, so it is redundant. The judgement is made once at formalisation, ALC is decidable, and every clause of both A and B holds.

The two statements address different things. a defines the economy figure as |Σ'| minus the size of the smallest subset equivalent to Σ'. b says how redundancy (equivalence) is judged until a logic is chosen: a statistical verifier on the named three-model panel, comparing only elements that share a term. Nothing in a fixes the method for judging equivalence, so b can supply it. Concrete case: no logic has been chosen yet. Σ' holds two traceable elements that share the term 'export' and have no other violations. The versioned decision question, with typed yes and no criteria, is sent through the OpenRouter Decisions API. microsoft/microsoft-decision-1.1 repeats its output exactly, so it is run once; the other two models are run three times each. The panel answers 'not redundant'. The smallest equivalent subset is therefore Σ' itself, and economy = 2 − 2 = 0. Every clause of both statements holds.

Statement a defines what counts as a violation for each figure, including 'each minimal unsatisfiable subset of elements' under fit. Statement b defines how contradiction is judged until a logic is chosen: `anthropic/claude-opus-5.5` at temperature 0, with the hashed template, sent one term-sharing pair at a time. b sets the procedure and a sets the scoring, so they do not conflict. Example: elements E1 'The report is due Monday' and E2 'The report is due Friday' share the term 'report'. The pair is sent alone, and the model replies 'contradiction', naming the two due dates. {E1,E2} then counts as one fit violation, and economy computes Σ' without E1 and E2. Every other term-sharing pair gets a schema-valid 'compatible' reply with an example, and no transport failure occurs, so verification is complete. b does not say that only pairs can be unsatisfiable, and a does not say how unsatisfiability is detected. Whether pairwise checking misses larger unsatisfiable sets is a question of method adequacy, not a logical clash.

Statement a lists which violations exist under each figure. Statement b says how a candidate's detected violations are scored and when the candidate passes. Neither requirement conflicts with the other. Example: there is one corpus, and it holds a single artefact. That artefact has one element, an INTENT element. It also has one definition, D1. D1 uses its own term, so it is traceable through INTENT. D1 has no other violations: no vague words, no duplicates, nothing unsatisfiable, and economy is 0. The true set is therefore {(form, D1, definition uses its own term)}. The candidate outputs exactly that set, so the symmetric-difference error is 0. It gives the same output on both runs, so it passes. One possible tension is that economy is a size rather than an itemised list. This does not matter here: economy is 0, and b's identification by figure, element and detail is satisfied.

The two statements cover different parts of one scheme and fit together. Statement a sets the scoring rule: an unweighted sum of violations, where an element counts in every figure it breaks, and zero means impeccable. Statement b says how two figures, contradiction and redundancy, become countable once elements are written in a decidable description logic. Concrete example: an artefact with three DL axioms, A ⊑ B, B ⊑ C and A ⊑ C, judged once at formalisation time. The set is satisfiable, so there is no minimal unsatisfiable subset and the contradiction count is 0. A ⊑ C is entailed by the other two, so it breaks the redundancy figure once. Slop = 0 + 1 = 1, with no weights, so the artefact is not impeccable. If the redundant axiom is removed, slop is 0 and the artefact is impeccable. Every clause of both statements holds in this example.

The statements cover different things. a says how violations are tallied: each element counts once in every figure it breaks, the counts are summed with no weights, and an artefact is impeccable exactly when the sum is zero. b says how one figure, redundancy, is detected until a logic is chosen: a versioned yes/no question with typed yes/no criteria, sent through the OpenRouter Decisions API to the three named pinned models. A model whose output repeats exactly runs once and any other model runs three times, and only elements sharing a term are compared. Neither statement limits the other. Example: an artefact has elements E1 and E2, which share the term 'cache', and E3, which shares no term with them. Only E1 and E2 are sent to the panel. Say microsoft-decision-1.1 is exactly repeatable and runs once, and the other two models run three times each. The panel answers 'redundant', so E1 and E2 each break the redundancy figure, adding 2 violations. E1 also breaks one other figure, adding 1. Slop = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3, with no weights, so the artefact is not impeccable. If the panel had answered 'no' and no other figure were broken, slop would be 0 and the artefact impeccable. Every clause of both statements holds.

The two statements cover different things. a defines how violations are counted and summed into slop. b defines how contradiction is judged before a logic is chosen. Example satisfying both: an artefact has three elements, E1, E2 and E3. E1 and E2 share a term, and that pair is sent alone, using the specified template, to anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 at temperature 0. The reply is a schema-valid contradiction that names the conflicting requirements. E3 shares no term with any other element, so no other pair is sent, and no refer, schema failure or transport failure occurs. The figures are then counted purely with no weights. E1 and E2 each break the contradiction figure, and no element breaks any other figure. The slop is the unweighted sum of 2, so the artefact is correctly not impeccable. If the reply had instead been compatible, with an example satisfying both elements, the sum would be 0 and the artefact impeccable. Neither statement says how incomplete verification affects the sum, and that silence is not a conflict.

The statements govern different things and do not conflict. Statement a defines slop: each element counts once in every figure it breaks, an artefact's slop is the unweighted sum of its violations across all figures, and an artefact is impeccable exactly when that sum is zero. Statement b says the statistical verifier is evaluated against a corpus whose slop is known, just as candidates are. Concrete example: build a corpus of three artefacts. Artefact X has one element that breaks figures F1 and F2, which counts twice, so its slop is 2. Artefact Y has one violation in F3, so its slop is 1. Artefact Z has no violations, so its slop is 0 and it is impeccable. These known slop values are fixed by a's unweighted rule. Evaluate the verifier by comparing its outputs with these known values, using the same procedure that candidates go through. Every clause of a holds (pure counting, unweighted sum, impeccable iff zero), and every clause of b holds (the verifier is evaluated, the corpus has known slop, and the evaluation matches how candidates are treated).

The two statements define different things that fit together: (a) scores artefacts by an unweighted violation count, and (b) scores a detector candidate against the true violation set. Example: a single corpus contains artefact X and artefact Y. In X, element e breaks figures F1 and F2. The true violations are (F1,e,d1) and (F2,e,d2), so e counts in both figures. X's slop is 1+1=2, so X is not impeccable. Y has no violations, so its slop is 0 and it is impeccable. Candidate C outputs exactly {(F1,e,d1),(F2,e,d2)} on this corpus. The symmetric difference with the true set is empty, so C's error is 0 on every corpus. C gives identical output on two runs, so C passes. Every clause of both statements holds.

B covers only the period before a logic is chosen; A describes what happens once elements are written as formulas in a decidable logic. Example: at first no logic is chosen. Redundancy between elements that share a term is judged by a versioned yes/no question with typed yes and no criteria, sent through the OpenRouter Decisions API to the three pinned models; a model whose output repeats exactly runs once, and the others run three times each. Later a description logic is chosen and the elements are formalised. Contradictions are then counted as minimal unsatisfiable subsets, and an element is redundant when the rest entails it. Each judgement is made once at formalisation and recorded, so verification gives way to formalisation as A says. Nothing in A forbids an interim statistical method, and nothing in B rules out the later move.

Statement b applies only 'until a logic is chosen'. Statement a states what the logic must be (decidable) and names description logics only as the candidate, so a has not chosen one yet. Example: no logic has been selected. For now, each pair of elements sharing a term is sent alone to anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 at temperature 0 with the hash-identified template. A reply of refer is escalated to the user. A schema or transport failure leaves verification incomplete and counts as no decision. Later, a decidable description logic is adopted and elements are written as formulas. A contradiction is then a minimal unsatisfiable subset, an element is redundant when the rest entails it, and the judgement is made once during formalisation and recorded. Two apparent tensions are differences between the interim and target regimes, not conflicts: b's pairwise checks versus a's subsets of any size, and b's judgement during verification versus a's move to formalisation.

Example: in a formalisation step, models (N samples, k required to agree) translate each element into a description-logic formula. That judgement is made once and recorded with the input hash, template hash, models, N and k. Contradictions (minimal unsatisfiable subsets) and redundancy (an element entailed by the rest) are then computed mechanically with a decidable reasoner. A later verification reads the record and asks for a fresh judgement only if the input or template hash has changed.
